speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

As a matter of privilege, I wish to draw the attention of the House to an article which appeared in the Toronto Globe of yesterday which among many others misstatements, contains the following :
In addition, there is a strong hydro-electric wing of the Government's support which is said to be bitterly hostile to aiding the Mackenzie interests while the hydro-electric project of Ontario, which Hon. Adam Beck has carried on from its inception against the active antagonism of what is called the ' Mackenzie electrical ring,' is given the go-by. This element is said to include Mr. Gordon Wilson, of Wentworth, Mr. Donald Sutherland, of South Oxford, Mr. William Smith, of South Ontario, Mr. W. A. Clarke, of North Wellington, and Mr. J. H. Fisher, of Brant.
I simply wish to say that, as far as I am concerned, there is not the slightest foundation foT that statement; it is absolutely untrue. I am only sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the rules of the House prevent me from characterizing this statement in the language which I would like

to use, and which I have already used outside the House.

Through the customary lack of veracity that so often characterizes the Toronto Globe, I' am placed in the same category with the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Fisher). I would like to read another paragraph in the article to which my hon. friend has already alluded:
Other members who tor the past few weeks have been prominent in well defined rumours connecting them with outspoken opposition to the deal are. Mr. Andrew Broder, of Dundas, who stated that he was not present at to-day's caucus, but had informed Premier Borden personally as to his position on the matter; Mr. Bernard Hepburn, of Prince Edward; Colonel J. A. Currie, of North Simcoe; Mr. F, N. Rhodes, of Cumberland, N.S. ; Mr. W. A. Boys, of South Simcoe; Mr. J. A. M. Armstrong, North York; Mr. J. A. Best, of Dufferin; Mr. A. C. Macdonell, South Toronto; Dr. M. Steele, South Perth; and Mr. H. J. Walker, of Northumberland.
The article is false on the face of it because it states that for the past few weeks these members have been outspoken in their criticism of the deal. Speaking for myself, I did not know what the deal would be until a few days ago, so this article is false like so many other articles appearing in the Toronto Globe. I wish to take this opportunity of characterizing that statement, so far as I am concerned, as a deliberate falsehood.

I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the statement read from the Toronto Globe by the hon. member for Brant, in which my name is included. I may say that the Canadian Northern railway have no warmer friend either in this House or out of it than I have been. Everything in that statement is untrue.

I also wish to state that the article, so far as I am concerned, is entirely untrue; and I want it distinctly understood that I am entirely in accord with the stand the Government has taken in regard to the matter.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege in order to show how rapidly a falsehood can spread. I wish to read from the Daily Sentinel Review of Woodstock, published in the county in which I live, an article which is as follows:
Despatches from Ottawa this morning state that there is a strong hydro-electric ring of Conservative members opposed to the granting of $45,000,000 to Mackenzie and Mann interests

in the Canadian Northern railway. , These members are opposed on the ground that the hydro-electric radial plan was set aside by the Government while Mackenzie and Mann are being favoured. Among these members, so the despatches state, is Donald Sutherland, representative for South Oxford.
I wish to state, Mr. Speaker, that in so far as I am concerned there is no foundation for this despatch which they claim came from Ottawa. As has already been pointed out 'by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Fisher) and the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith), there is absolutely no ground for it in this instance, and I think it is an abuse of the privileges of the representatives of the press in this House that they will send out wilfully, deliberately, and of malice aforethought, despatches which they must know to- be false.
Would the- hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question? Is the hon. gentleman in favour of the resolution on 'the Order Paper in connection with Mackenzie -and Mann?
I will answer that at the proper time.

In regard to the article from -yesterday's Globe read by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Fisher), wherein my name is used, I want to say that the statement in absolutely untrue. I never gave any reason to anybody, either directly or indirectly, which would justify the use of my name- in that article. I -did not know anything about what d-e-al was going to be made until it was brought up in the caucus and I am satisfied that the Government has made the very best deal they possibly could. I think that this article is on a par with the greater part of the articles that appear in the Globe.

With respect to the
article in the Toronto Globe as read by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Fisher) and the hon. member for North York (Mr. Armstrong), in so far as it mentions my name, I wish to borrow the adjective used by these hon. gentlemen in respect to that article and to say 'that it is absolutely false. Perhaps I might conclude by -saying that I believe these proposals are- as good as the Government could possibly have made, and they have my heartiest approval.

306. Marble, sawn or sand rubbed, not polished; granite, sawn; paving blocks of stone; flag stone and building stone, other than marble or granite, sawn on not more than two sides-British preferential, 15 per cent, intermediate, 20 per cent; general, 20 per cent.
Is this an increase or a decrease ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is somewhat an important item. I think my hon. friend will understand it better if I give a brief explanation as to this item and the two succeeding items. The rates fixed in respect to the articles mentioned in this item are the same as to British Preferen-tion and General as before. In other words: Rough stone and stone sawn on not more than two sides may be brought into Canada, when the new tariff goes into effect, at the same rate as before. The rates have been increased on building stone, under item 306a, other than marble or granite sawn on more than two sides but not sawn on more than four sides, and item 306b says:
306b. Building stone, other than marble or granite, planed, turned, cut or further manufactured than sawn on four sides.
We have increased the duty upon the more finished stone. On stone sawn only on two sides the rate is the same as before. On building stone sawn on two sides, but not sawn on more than four sides, the rate has been fixed at 10 cents Preferential, and 15 cents General per 100 pounds.
What would that be ad valorem ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would vary. The cheapest stone is worth 55 cents per cubic foot, and some other stone will run as high as one dollar per cubic foot. A cubic foot weighs about 160 pounds. The increase in the tariff is on the more finished article. Stone sawn on more than two sides and finished, under item 306b, will run from 30 per cent to 40 per cent ad valorem,
the previous rates being twenty per cent British preference.

I desire to speak on this item on account of certain information I have received respecting a public building in the town of Walkerville. I myself know nothing about the building. The minister, in discussing this item in his Budget speech, as reported in ' Hansard/ said:
There is very great difficulty in administering the tariff to-day on account of the difficulty in ascertaining the value of finished, dressed stone coming in as an import. The average ad valorem of the specific rate which I have quoted is 30 per cent upon turned, planed, cut or further finished stone. I propose a rate of 45 cents per 100 pounds, which is equal to 30 per cent ad valorem.
As I understand it, this is done in the interest of the stonecutters of the Dominion of Canada. There is a quarry very close to Canada, at Bedford, Indiana, from which a great deal of this stone is imported in the finished state into Canada for public buildings. It would cost little more to bring in this stone in the finished state and pay the duty on it at the old rate than it would to bring the rough stone in and have it cut here. The argument is that, if the Government desire to help the stonecutters of the Dominion, they should prohibit the importation of the harder kinds of stone of which there are a great many quarries in the Dominion, principally in New Brunswick. In the Dominion there are no quarries of the kind of stone.on which the minister proposes to increase the duty. In regard to the public building at Walkerville, my informant writes me as follows:
Herewith quotations covering all the stone for the Walkerville post office, f.o.b., Bedford, Indiana:
Alternate No. 1 includes the two courses for the foundation and step sides:-Stone, f.o.b., Bedford, price, $372; old duty, $74.20; new duty, $266.40; difference, $192.20.
Alternate No. 2 includes the steps:-Stone, f.o.b., Bedford, price, $187; old duty, $37.40 ; new duty, $133.65 ; difference, $96.25.
Alternate No. 3 includes the base course and copping on step walls:-Stone, f.o.b., Bedford, price, $457; old duty, $91.40 ; new duty, $327.60 ; difference, $266.20.
Alternate No. 4 includes all above the base course:-Stone, f.o.b., Bedford, price, $7,635 ; old duty, $1,727 ; new duty, $6,069.60 ; difference, $4,342.60
I am merely quoting this building as an instance where this stone is used, to show the difference that will be made in the price providing the change in the tariff brought down by the minister goes through. If these figures are correct-and my informant is a practical stone man who takes contracts for

this class of work in a great many places in Ontario-the minister will see that it is practically a prohibitive duty. From these figures and taking the facts as they stand, namely, that this stone can be procured in the way I have mentioned, and that there are many quarries of the harder stone in Canada, it appears to me that, if this duty were put on the hard stone and left off this * stone, it would be of more advantage to the stonecutters than the duty which the minister proposes to impose. We have an almost inexhaustible supply of granite at St. John, St. George, and other parts of the Dominion. If the duty on this cut stone were lowered to a reasonable amount and not made, as it is at present, absolutely prohibitive, the object for which the tariff is increased would be fairly well brought about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that, on account of the noise that has prevailed in the House, I have been unable to follow my hon. friend as I should have liked, but I gather in a general way that he is arguing that this duty is prohibitive and that the price of finished stone will be greatly increased to the consumer in Canada. We have not increased the duty upon rough stone, or stone sawn on not more than two sides; that stone will come in, whether from the quarry in the United States that my hon. friend has in mind or .from other United States quarries, at the same rate as before. What 1 intend to accomplish by this increase is, that the stone so brought in shall as far as possible be cut and finished in Canada by Canadian stonecutters. This matter has been before the Government for many years, and no item in the tariff has been more persistently or more earnestly brought to my attention since I have been Minister of Finance than this item relating to cut stone. I have here so much material that I would not know how to use it all, and I would not think of putting even a fraction of it upon ' Hansard.' I have here, for example, a bundle of petitions with respect to this matter, signed by members of the Stonecutting and Quarry Trades of Canada and by builders' exchanges from' all parts of Canada. I will just read the endorsement upon this bundle of petitions, which bears the superscription of the Montreal Builders' Exchange :
We endorse the petition being presented by the Stonecutting and Quarry Trades of Canada. We desire to have the duty on all kinds of

building stone except rough quarry blocks placed on a properly protective basis in the interest of quarrymen, stonecutters and stone contractors throughout the Dominion of Canada, namely, 65 cents per cubic foot, to be measured at its extreme dimensions.
My hon. friend will observe that the tariff modifications which we propose do not go nearly so far as that; but the allied stone industry of Canada, that is, the stonemen- the stonecutters and the stone contractors- have asked the Government, not only once but repeatedly, to give them a reasonable degree of protection so that the men engaged in the stonecutting trade, who from time to time, especially in the winter, are out of work in Canada, shall have the opportunity of dressing and cutting the stone used in the erection of buildings in Canada. If the stone to which my hon. friend refers comes in in the rough or dressed on not more than two sides, there is no reason why the cost to the consumers, that is to say, the parties, firms, corporations, or municipalities, erecting buildings, should be more than the cost of the raw material plus the cost of the labour bestowed upon that by Canadian artisans. I do not see that it can be any more than that. I have received requests for the revision of the tariff in respect of this item from the Journeymen Stone Cutters' Association of America, from the following branches: St. Marc des Carrieres, Quebec; Quebec city, Montreal, St. Martin, Neilsonville, Terrebonne, Belanger Village, St. Michel, London, Ontario, Niagara Falls, Port Arthur, Ottawa, Kingston, Peterborough, Toronto, Winnipeg, St. Boniface, Tyndall, Calgary, Edmonton, Moosejaw, Regina, Vancouver and Victoria. Builders associations and builders exchanges in various places have also asked for this, putting it on the ground that they desire to have the opportunity of dressing and finishing the stone brought into Canada for use in the construction of our buildings. My own view is that if stone is brought in in the rough, the rate of duty being increased only on the dressed stone, the only increase that, could take place to the consumer would be the cost of the labour bestowed by Canadian artisans after it is brought in, and the legislation proposed, whether well designed or not, is to accomplish that object. It is in the interest of the artisans, the stonecutters of Canada, and indirectly, as I stated in the Budget, it will be of advantage to Canadian quarrymen. I desire to read for the information of the committee extracts from the petitions that have

been received by me from the various stonecutters associations I have mentioned.
If the duty on rough stone is not to be increased where does the advantage to the quarrymen come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The advantage will be an indirect advantage. It will make generally for the development of the stonecutting in (Canada. The quarry industry in Canada is not in a very satisfactory condition, nor is the stonecutting industry. My hon. friend seemed to doubt whether this legislation would be of any benefit to the stonecutter of Canada. I have a letter from the Journeymen Stonecutters' Association, signed by the secretary, and dated 24th of March, 1914, which is in part as follows:
I was instructed by the Stonecutters' Union to write in regard to tho stone tariff. We have no doubt that you have read the article in a recent issue of the Montreal Daily Mail in which it is stated that half the wealth of a nation is in its buildings. Uor a great many of the buildings mentioned in the article stone is brought from the United States ready to set though there was a large number of stonecutters around here looking for work. .We think that if the tariff was raised on cut stonev contractors would cut their stone in Canada instead of getting it from the United States and in that way employ Canadian stonecutters and other connected with stone.

According to that letter, they hope that the stone will be cut in Canada. But the trouble is that the stone taken out at Bedford is in the rough, but it is allowed to be dressed there, they only pay freight on the dressed stone, and so they can get it to the point where it is to be used much cheaper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is one of the very reasons for this legislation. The freight upon stone, whether rough or dressed, is according to its weight, and in the dressing the reduction of weight is considerable. The customs tariff hitherto has been uniform, being 20 per cent upon stone whether rough or dressed. If stone was brought into Canada in the rough, and a higher freight charge had to be paid than if it was brought in dressed, the result of the tariff, so far .as it was designed to benefit the stonecutting industry in Canada was completely nullified, because the difference in freight more than neutralized the tariff advantage which was evidently the design of Parliament to give under the item in question. There is no doubt about this in the minds of the stonecutters of Canada. If the hon. gentleman will look through the mass of petitions and 197
correspondence, extending over two or three years, that I have here, he can come to only one conclusion, and that is tfiat there is no doubt in the minds of the stonecutters that it would be of advantage to them. This legislation is brought down because it .is urged upon tne Government, and the Government desire to bring about a benefit to the stonecutting industry in Canada.
Is it sound economy to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Absolutely, I believe. Why should not stone be cut in this country and dressed by Canadian workmen?

I have never
given much consideration to the matter, but I should rather be inclined to believe that it would be of advantage to the country, and especially to the artisans and consumers, that -stone should be made as cheap as possible, and that therefore it should be on the free list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Dressed stone?
All kinds of stone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course, it is open to my hon. friend to put forward that view. But the quarry owners of the country have a very different opinion. My hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) argues that this does not benefit the quarrymen of Canada. So, my hon. friend from West Lambton and my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) are evidently wide apart upon the question.
I simply asked how it benefits the quarrymen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me ask my hon. friend, would he be in favour of taking the duty off stone, having regard to the condition of the quarry industry in Canada?
I have not given consideration to1 that matter.
How about the interest of the consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will come to that. The tariff has not been changed with regard to rough'stone or stone sawn on not more-than two sides. So, if the stone is cut in Canada by Canadian workmen, at reasonable rates, and if the stonecutting industry can thereby be developed I do not see how the consumer is disadvantaged. It seems to me a wise tariff policy to admit raw material in on the free list or at a low rate, and that the finishing of the raw material



into the manufactured product should, as far as possible, be done by Canadians. Now, this matter seems to be of considerable interest to my hon. friend from West Lamb-ton, and so I propose to read from the petitions we have received from the builders exchanges throughout Canada. The following representations appear in these petitions :
The statement given herewith constitutes the petition of stonecutting and quarry trade section of the Montreal Builders' Exchange. Our body desires to have the duty on all kinds of building stone, except rough quarry blocks, placed on a properly protected basis in the interests of quarrymen, stonecutters and stone contractors throughout the Dominion of Canada. Copies of this statement are now being signed from one end of the country to the other, and will be forwarded to you in due course before the meeting of Parliament.
The languishing industry for whose life we plead is that of the stone quarrymen, the stonecutters and the stone contractors of Canada. The Government statistics report that last year there were already more than sixty quarries in operation in the West alone. We who represent the capital invested in them know better than any one else under what immense difficulties they are kept alive-where they are not already practically closed-but these figures show the immense possibilities of this industry in a part of the country where industries are scarce; and these possibilities are of course quite as great-if not greater-in other provinces. Quarrying is an industry exceptionally localized and native. The very weight of the material handled should rivet it to the soil. That it does not do so in Canada, with its abundance of good stone, is proof positive thrjt we are suffering from an altogether unusual and unjust competition.
There was a time when Canada quarried her own stone and even invaded successfully the American market. In many of the great American cities there rise to-day monuments to these victories of the past. The finest buildings of that time were built with Canadian stone; and when the American owners desire even now to enlarge or alter them, they must still come to our quarries to get similar material. But the shrewd and ambitious Americans were very unwilling to be dependent upon a foreign country for their building material. So the McKinley tariff put a duty of 50 per cent on building stone, except marble, and 65 cents a cubic foot on marble, with a view to shutting out the Canadian product and creating an American stone industry.
That duty did its work. Protection protected. A great American stone industry grew up which now not only satisfies the immense American demand, but dominates the Canadian situation and is slowly grinding our stone industry to powder. Our protection against this highly protected and splendidly organized and well equipped foreign industry is only 20 per cent on the face of the tariff; and-as we shall show- is really very much less than that. The 20 per cent is the duty on all building stone, sawn or dressed, which the customs authorities rule covers practically all American manufactured stone imported. There is a duty of 35 per cent 
on manufactures of marble or granite, and of 30 per cent on manufactures of stone; but under the ruling of our Customs Department, these duties are almost wholly inoperative.
The reason for this is also one of the reasons why the new American industry is so successful. By modern methods stone is manufactured for shipment when it is sawn. The up-to-date diamond saws render it unnecessary to manufacture it any further. It is then ready for the building and comes in under the 20 per cent duty. So the Americans are able to send in their manufactured stone under the description ' sawn ' and escape with no more than a duty of 20 per cent. This 20 per cent, however, is levied upon their invoices-not upon the prices with which we must compete. They have an adroit system of bookkeeping by which they show that various other charges than the value of the stone are incorporated in the price they charge in Canada-as, for example, freight, cartage, insurance, etc. These items are taken from the total and' they pay duty only on what they will admit is the quarry value of their stone. The result is that they are 'dumping' most flagrantly all the time.
And this whole question is a subject which deeply concerns Canadian labour. Formerly we had the best quarrymen and stonecutters on the continent. When the McKinley tariff drew our industry over to the United States, our workmen followed it. We would lijte to get them back. But they will not come back until we can offer them permanent employment and we can only do this when we are assured of our own market. We shall be compelled to pay them higher wages than they get in the United States, as the climatic conditions there permit of more continuous work during the winter months.
I desire to read the concluding paragraphs of this petition, which was signed, as I say, by the stonecutters' and builders' exchanges in all parts of Canada:
As we have intimated before, we are satisfied that no system of ad valorem duties will adequately protect our industry. Our foreign competitors are too fertile in devising means to avoid the intended effect of such duties. They have already succeeded in nullifying the plain intention of the Canadian Parliament by making our 30 and 35 per cent duties inoperative; and they have gone very much further, and, by a system of manipulated invoices, greatly reduced the effect of even the 20 per cent duty they nominally pay. Hence we are in favour of establishing a duty which will not be a high percentage on the proper and honest value of the article in question, but which will prevent misunderstanding and fraud. This should be a specific duty; and we should suggest a specific tariff of 65 cents a cubic foot on building stone of any kind, sawn, dressed, hewn, polished or otherwise manufactured. This is the very lowest minimum duty which can be of the slightest service to us; and we have named it badly with a view to taking the Government into our confidence and- laying all our cards on the table. In order to make this effective at all, it must also be enacted that the stone be measured at its extreme dimensions, thus forestalling trouble in the matter of measurements.
If we are granted this protection, we think that we can confidently guarantee the Govern-

311P
ment that a widespread and important stone industry will grow up in Canada. Once more our cities will be built of Canadian stone manufactured by Canadian labour. The great buildings which are now rising in every centre in the land from the Atlantic to the Pacific will be monuments to Canadian natural wealth, to Canadian progress and to Canadian skill.
This legislation, whether wise or unwise, has been brought down by the Government by reason of the strong, earnest and continuous representations made to them by the stonecutters of Canada. They say that the present tariff affords them no protection and that they see no reason why the stonecutters of Canada should not dress and cut the stone used in Canadian buildings. II the stone of quarries not only of the United States but of other countries is desired for use in Canadian buildings, that stone may be brought in under the existing rates and may be dressed and further manufactured by the Canadian artisan. Person-
4 p.m. ally, I cannot see why the cost of the stone, if not manufactured on more than two sides, should be increased beyond the cost of the raw material, plus the cost of the labour which would be bestowed upon it in Canada. It is a fact that, notwithstanding the enormous building activity in Canada, there are frequent and prolonged periods of unemployment for the Canadian stonecutters, when they drift across the line in the winter, whereas they might be continuously employed here. It does seem to me that if any protective legislation is justifiable, legislation of this character can certainly be justified upon the grounds that I have mentioned.

I received a letter from
the proprietor of a quarry in my county and, although it does not necessarily express my own opinion, I would like the minister to consider what this quarry owner has to say with regard to this increase of duty. The letter is as follows:
This proposed change is solely in the interests of the large cut stone contractors, as the duty on rough blocks, 15 per cent, and on stone sawn on two sides, 20 per cent, is left unchanged. On the other hand, the duty is to be raised on stone sawn on four sides or further manufactured.
That, I think, is an error; the duty is not to bo raised if the stone is not to be sawn on more than four sides. Item 306b means that there is a duty of 15 cents per hundred pounds on stone sawn on two sides, including also stone sawn on four sides. The 45 cent rate is on stone further manufactured than sawn on four sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That last statement I think is correct; further manufactured than sawn, on four sides is the higher rate.
How does that help the stone cutters if you allow it in sawn on the four sides?

My correspondent proceeds :
On the other hand the duty is to be raised on stone sawed on four sides or further manufactured. If there is to be a change in the tariff, surely the quarrying industry-developing our own resources-is as worthy of increased protection as the cut stone industry-working largely on imported stone.
As far as the stonecutter, as we know him, is concerned, the proposed change will make little difference to him. His work is mostly on local stone, as Montreal limestone and Maritime province stones, where the cutting is largely done by hand. On the other hand the large contractors working with imported stone, do most of their work with machinery.
We have properties in your country that we propose to develop as soon as we get the necessary capital. It is the opinion of myself, and of very many people-architects and others- that Miramichi stone is the best and the most beautiful building stone on the continent. The Langevin Block, Ottawa, Lord Strathcona's house and the Birk's building, Montreal, are well known examples of work in which this stone has been used.
Every hoa. gentleman present knows the stone because it is used in the Langevin block in Ottawa. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister in the hope that he may consider if he is treating our quarry men fairly in raising the duty on stone manufactured further than sawn on four sides to 45 cents and not increasing it on ordinary rough stone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is it the opinion of my
hon. friend that the tariff o,m rough stone finished on any more than two sides should be increased?

It is the opinion of my
friend who is writing to me, and I am not expressing my personal opinion on the matter. My correspondent is a quarry man interested in a quarry in my county and I want the minister to consider his representation of these matters. If I were asked an opinion personally I would say not to increase the duty, to leave the matter as it is.

The more this matter is looked into the more we will discover that it is exactly like other particular changes in the tariff, in the interest of the big manufacturers of cut stone, not in the interest of the consumer. There is

no question whatever that if this1 increased, duty is levied you practically shut off all competition from outside and you will raise the cost of every building in which cut stone is used in the future. While possibly a larger amount of the work that is done will be done by Canadian stone-cutters, the result will be, in the end, an increase in the cost of building with cut stone, so that under the increased duty the Canadian stone-cutters will cut less stone than at the present. During the Budget debate I drew the attention of the minister to one particular case. I do not pretend to be posted on this matter and I would be most averse to taking work away from the Canadian stone cutter. But there is more than the Canadian stone-cutter to consider. One of the reports that the minister has just read pointed out that there were 60 quarries in the West, which, according to the report, are in a languishing condition. Why are they in a languishing condition ? Because their prices are -simply prohibitive. They want to have -matters in their own hand now and their prices under the increased duty will be practically prohibitive. I drew the attention of the House to one circumstance that *came under my own knowledge in connection with an office building in which I was interested which was being erected in Regina. They wanted cut stone in the front of the building. They instructed the architect to get prices on cut stoRe and to get the stone in Canada if possible. They sent down to Winnipeg where there are several quarries in operation and asked for prices. We got the stone delivered in Regina, freight and duty paid, for $1,600 less than the amount of the Canadian tenders, although the , American tenderer paid the duty and freight two or three times as far as the freight from the quarries near Winnipeg to Regina. The stone near Winnipeg is first-class stone and would have been entirely satisfactory, but the prices were exorbitant; and if the Government now steps in and shuts off all competition a few of the large stone cutting firms will reap all the benefit, there is no question about that. They will make more money, but I claim that the Canadian quarry man, the Canadian stone-cutter will not reap any benefit and the Canadian consumer will get it where my hon. friend is generally inclined to give it to him, in the neck.
Simply because the increased price will shut out the use of cut stone for trimming buildings. They will use brick and cement instead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that this tariff change will not inure to the benefit of the stone-cutters.
Not in the end.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The opinion of the journeymen stone-cutters themselves ought to be as valuable at least as that of my hon. friend. I hold here petitions signed by stone-cutters associations from all parts of Canada. Many of- these have been sent in to me by members who have been interested in this subject. I deem it of so much importance, in view of the statements made by my hon. friend that this will not inure to the benefit of the stonecutters, that I am going to place one of these petitions on ' Hansard.' I will read it, as my hon. friend will find it interesting:
We, the officers of the Journeymen Stonecutters Association of North America, Montreal branch, have been authorized by a meeting of council held in Montreal on November 6, 1912, to call to your notice and ask you to give your favourable consideration to the following request:
We might state that we have a membership of about seven hundred mechanics, stonecutters and carvers in Montreal, and there are fully as many more scattered around in the province of Quebec, besides quarrymen and helpers employed in conjunction with us. Our very existence is being threatened by the invasion of stone imported from the United States, cut and finished, ready for erection in buildings owing to the present conditions of the tariff which does not protect our industries. This is caused largely by the improvements in machinery and transportation, but if the tariff was framed to allow only rough stone to be imported we are convinced that more machinery would he installed in Canada and our industry would get its natural expansion instead of the trade going from us.
We have taken cognizance of the petition dated October 8, 1912, presented by the Montreal Builders' Exchange. We agree with this petition and indorse it in every way. It would be useless to go further into details which are so well defined. It is in our interests as well as in the interests of capital that the cut stone and quarry industries get the protection asked for.
It would give us much steadier work if the tariff was adjusted as our employers would adjust their plants for winter work. Many large jobs have been cut outside -of Canada when members of our Union have been idle here. This applies all over Canada. The stonecutters of the West are in a worse position than we are.
The Canadian quarries are not being developed simply because they are unable to compete with the cut stone imported from outside. We know that we have the stone in Canada hut

the quarries have not heen worked and opened up. The quarries south of Canada were not developed until the great demand for cut stone came along; now we have an immense demand in Canada for first class buildings employing a lot of stone and we would request that the opportunity be given for the development of Canadian quarries. We have only scratched the surface of the rock in Canada and have not got down to the best layers of stone in any of the quarries- We would request our share of the expansion and prosperity which Canada is enjoying at the present time.
This petition is signed by journeymen's associations all over Canada. The journeymen should know where their interests lie, and when my hon. friend makes the assertion that this tariff change will not be of any benefit to the stonecutters of Canada,
I can only conclude that he pays not the slightest attention to the expression of their opinion, as given in the petition I have just read.
Does my hon. friend think that the stonecutters and quarry-men are the best judges in that matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The stonecutters are the best judges as to whether this particular legislation will advantage' them or not; as to whether it will have the effect of giving them employment in winter in finishing stone imported for use in buildings in Canada. My hon. friend has referred to the stone industry in the West. I agree with him that Canada ought to produce all the stone required for use in the construction of buildings throughout the Dominion. We have unlimited quantities of stone, but it is a fact that the quarrying industry of Canada has not developed as we might have expected. Complaint has been made that this is due to the fact that under the McKinley tariff Canadian stone was shut out almost entirely from the United States, and that by reason of the low Canadian tariff, cut stone was imported from the United States to meet the requirements of Canada. The result has been, according to the quarrymen's contention, that the Canadian quarries have not been developed.
In answer to the representations made by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) through the letter of his correspondent, I would say that the Government had repeated requests from the quarry interests to increase the duty not only upon finished stone, but upon rough stone. So far the Government has not seen fit to act' on these representations. What the correspondent of my hon. friend from Northumberland had in view was that the Government should be asked to increase
the duty upon rough stone, which as I have said, has not been done.
And sawn on four sides?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, sawn, not only on
two sides, but up to four sides. I do not know whether my hon. friend subscribes to the opinion held by his correspondent, but his correspondent undoubtedly asks that the duty on rough stone shall be increased in the interest of Canadian quarries. No doubt a good deal can be said for that view, but so far the Government has not brought down legislation to increase the duty upon rough stone. Whether we shall do so in the future or not I am unable at this moment to say. I have-been asked as to how this new legislation will benefit the Canadian quarrymen. I think the answer is supplied in the assertion of my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee) that if this legislation goes through, stone in the rough will not be imported. If stone in the rough is not imported, it is obvious that the stone required for Canadian purposes will be supplied from our own quarries, and indirectly, therefore, the Canadian quarry industry will be advantaged by this legislation.

If you make the duty
absolutely prohibitive-and I think the figures that I have quoted prove that it will be-would it not give the Canadian quarrymen power to charge just what they like for their stone, as in the case instanced by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff)? It would establish a monopoly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not admit that the
duty is prohibitive; 30 to 35 per cent is not generally regarded as prohibitive. An equal duty is imposed on many items in the tariff. My hon. friend must bear in mind that there are many qualities of stone, and that they vary as to price. Take building stone sawn on four sides, for instance; the cheapest is 55 cents per cubic foot, but it runs as high as a dollar. The average duty upon this is about 30 per cent.

Might I put it in another way? Taking the concrete case of the Walkerville building, if stone f.o.b Bedford costs $7,635, the duty under the old tariff would amount to $1,727; under the new tariff the duty would be $3,200. Does

the minister not consider that a prohibitive duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether
my hon. friend's figures are correct or not; all of us are fallible at times, and my hon. friend may be mistaken as to his figures. But whether correct or not, I would not admit that if a prohibitive duty -is imposed on an article that the cost to the Canadian consumer would be the cost of the article in a foreign market plus the duty, because that would presuppose that there was no competition within the tariff wall. I do not admit that for one moment. We have quarries all over Canada competing with each other. It has not been suggested that there is a combine among the quarrymen of Canada. On the contrary, there is competition. As long as the raw material is admitted at a reasonable rate of duty the only question that would arise, unless there is some understanding between all the quarrymen, is this: How much is the additional cost by reason of the fact that the raw material is finished in Canada by Canadian labour? I have not raised the rate upon rough stone and I have not raised the rate on stone sawn on two sides only. Therefore what question can arise? If the rough stone is finished in the United States the cost at the place where it is manufactured in the United States is the cost of the raw material plus the labour. It 'is precisely the same in Canada. The cost will be the cost of the rough stone, or stone sawn on not more than two sides, imported into Canada plus the cost of the Canadian labour bestowed upon it. The object of this resolution is to bring it about that by a reasonable tariff the Canadian stonecutting industry may get the advantage and the men may get work during the winter months who are now walking the streets idle.	* gj
Bedford, Indiana, limestone sawed four sides, 55 cents per cubic foot, f.o.b., quarry.
In respect to stone further manufactured than sawn on four sides the practice in the United States is to sell the stone on the basis of the rough stone plus a charge per hour for the work performed thereon. It is, therefore, impossible to state the exact price charged per cubic foot on finished stone, the requirements of no two customers being alike; the patterns in each case being different with the result that the machine work cost more on one than on the other. Invoices have been examined and the average is about $2 per cubic foot.
The case which has been brought to the attention of my hon. friend may be an ex-[Mr. Pardee. J
treme one. It, is perfectly obvious from this statement that the prices vary. We must look at the average price, and the statement made here is that the average price is about $2 per cubic foot. This duty then would run from 30 to 40 per cent on the finished stone. Bough stone will remain precisely as it is under the present tariff.

The minister will admit that it is much more expensive to finish stone by all hand work than by the planer. If it is a fact that there is no stone on this side on which the planer can be used it must cost more to the consumer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why can they not plane it here?
They do not do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why not?

I suppose there must be some good reason why there is no stone produced in Canada that is planed here and as a consequence it must be all done by hand work which makes it more expensive to the consumer. The minister says that, provided the duty is put on as he proposes, even according to the figures I have quoted on the Walkerville building, it does not necessarily mean that as a consequence the consumer will have to pay whatever charge may ibe asked of him by the producers of Canada because there is competition, between the producers and as a result the price will be kept down. But, if my figures are correct, they simply go to show that it will be no time at all, because this tariff is prohibitive of importation, before there is a combine amongst the quarrymen of the Dominion and they will simply lift the prices to whatever height they see fit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then we can deal with it.

It just brings me back to the conclusion that the very minute you put a prohibitive duty upon any article that is used by the public, that minute you make it possible to form a combine and allow the combine to charge what they like to the consumer.

My hon. friend from
Lambton (Mr. Pardee) seems to have based his argument entirely upon the stone that is supposed to enter into the federal building at Walkerville. From what I can gather from the specifications, the stone that is to enter into the construction of that building is Roman stone which is a kind

of artificial stone manufactured in Toronto and which will not come from Bedford. Application has already been made by some other parties who manufacture another kind of stone, which they claim is equally as good as Eoman stone, to have their product included in the specifications and the matter is now being considered by the arehitectis in the Department of Public Works. Therefore, I am rather inclined to the view that my hon. friend has received bis information torn a! (wrong source and that the stone which will enter into the construction of this building will not come from the United States.
Mi'. PAEDEE: I did not say that it would come from the United States at all but my argument was based upon the figures which I have quoted and which come from a contractor who ha.s tendered upon the Walker-ville building.
You said that it would come from Bedford, Indiana?

Certainly, because if he
gets the contract the stone will come from Bedford. If a prohibitive duty goes on his tender cannot be considered for one moment and he is shut out.

I think my hon. friend
will agree that under the specifications which have been adopted by the department of Public Works the stone that is to be used is to be Eoman stone and that it cannot be the sandstone which comes from Indiana.

They will not allow
Eoman stone in Ontario, will they?
Oh, yes they will.

The minister mentioned a moment ago that he had not raised the duty on stone sawn on two sides. I infer from that, that he is in doubt as to whether the duty on stone sawn on four sides has: been raised. Would the minister mind telling me what the ad valorem rate would be equivalent to 15 cents per 100 pounds under item 306b?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have said that the average ad valorem rate is 30 per cent.
As I understood the minister had not raised the duty on stone sawn on four sides but as a matter of fact he has.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Well, I understand that
under the present tariff it comes in at a rate of 20 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
If 15 cents per 100 pounds is the equivalent of 30 per cent then I am wrong; the minister has raised it 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Then my correspondent is right and the minister has raised the duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Your correspondent is right in this:	We have raised the duty upon
stone that is sawn on more than two sid*i. On building stone we have made two classes; on stone that is sawn on more than two sides but not sawn on more than four sides we have made a rate of 15 cents peT 100 pounds. Then, under 306b, for
Building stone, other than marble or granite, planed, turned, cut or further manufactured than sawn on four sideswhich is cut stone, we have made a rate of 45 cents per 100 pounds.
I understood the minister to say that the ad valorem rate on stone sawn on four sides would be about 30 per cent. If that be true the cost of planing is very material.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Then the minister has
raised the duty on stone further finished than that to the extent of from 50 to 60 per cent, because it is three times as much on the further manufactured article, namely, 45 cents and it is raised 15 cents when it is manufactured to the extent of being sawn on four sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In reducing a specific duty to the ad valorem rate the cost of the article dealt with must be considered.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Stone sawn on four sides only is not nearly as expensive as stone that is planed and further finished. The result is that the 45 cents per 100 lb., which appears to my hon. friend to be such a substantial increase, is, I believe, having regard to the value of the stone to which it relates, less than the 15 cents per 100 lbs. rate on stone sawn on four sides only. Where my hon. friend is confused is, that he has failed to recognize the in

crease in value given to the stone by the cutting process to which it is subjected.

My hon. friend the minister considers that the stone-cutters and the large firms who deal in cut stone are a sufficient authority for him to grant their request when they place before him the wants of their business. From their statement of the ease, he increases the duty largely in accordance with their demand, but when the wheat growers of . Canada come to this Government and present their case, the minister and the Government do not consider that they know anything about their business. Their ideas are not considered at all; they are turned down and other interests considered when it comes to deal with their industry. That shows the difference in the treatment handed out on the one hand to the wheat growers of Canada and on the other to the big cut-stone concerns, who wish to shut out all competition and Charge any price they choose to the people who put up buildings in which cut stone is used.

Taking up the last point, I maintain that the hon. member for Assiniboia is clearly wrong. The wheat raisers of Canada, not considering the West alone, do not want free wheat. Some of the stonecutters of West Peterborough have been out of work for years because the duty has been too low, and for the same reason the stonecutters of the United States have been enjoying the employment that Canadians should have had. Why the Opposition will persist in dragging in the principle of protection and free trade at every available opportunity is more than I can understand, because it really ought to he evident to them by this time that, if you have an evenly, properly balanced system of protection, both the consumer and the producer are relatively in precisely the same position in which they were before that duty was put on. They are in exactly the same relative position as if there were free trade. My hon. friends opposite, however, do not seem to be able to grasp the simple mathematical proposition that if you add equals to equals the results are equal. Add the duty to all and all are equal. It is a very simple proposition, and my hon. friends ought to be able to grasp it. There is a difference as regards the outsider or the foreigner, but we are not legislating for the outsider or the foreigner; we are legislating for ourselves, IMr. W. T. White.]
and there is absolutely no difference between the relative position of the producer and the consumer when each producer, who is also a consumer, receives a fair measure of protection.
These stonecutters of West Peterborough are very desirous of having this legislation passed; and, consistently with the true policy of protection which is so widely and so well promulgated and directed in Canada, and which has resulted to the very great glory and benefit of Canada, I say that we should have this legislation and I hope it will be promptly passed without any further objection.

I desire to say a word or two on this question. I have, I suppose, in my county nearly all the quarries in Manitoba. There is at Garson, some thirty-five miles east of the city of Winnipeg, a plant that employs about 250 stonecutters; at least it did when it was in active operation. It is one of the largest quarries in Canada. During the presentation of the last Budget of the Hon. Mr. Fielding, I presented a petition from the stonecutters of Manitoba asking for increased protection, and pointing out that, if they did not get that protection, the industry in which they were engaged would be affected very materially. What has been the result in that institution? Owing to the fact that American stone could be brought in in competition with our own, that institution last year employed less than a quarter of the number it was employing before. The American stone was coming in in a finished condition; all the labour required to finish that stone being procured on the other side of the line. The dressing of the stone is the most valuable part of the work. The stonecutters, who are highly paid men, were leaving Garson, going to the other side of the line and building up industries there instead of in Canada. The protection now afforded to the stonecutters is, to my mind, a wise one.
I can very well understand how the case that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) gave us a moment ago in regard to the increased cost of stone at Regina might occur. I can believe there are cases where stone from the other side of the line can be brought in and manufactured in Canada cheaper than stone quarried at Garson, but I do not think there is any such difference in price as my hon. friend has quoted. So far as the case he has mentioned is com-cerned, he may be absolutely right. Any-

one knows that contractors, when tendering for supplying a certain quantity of stone for a building, are very liable to make mistakes or to ask a greater sum than they are justified in getting for a certain work, but that does not apply generally. On some of the finest buildings in Winnipeg, and before there was any attempt to increase the duty, the contractors were using our Manitoba stone which is as -good as any stone in America. This industry is surely worthy of being aided. I admit that it would be wrong to put a prohibitive duty on any article that would give any industry an opportunity to control the market. I do not, however, believe that this duty is prohibitive. The duty on sawn stone and on stone dressed on two sides has been increased only slightly. The rought stone still comes in at the old rate of 20 per cent. One of the hon. gentlemen pointed out that the fact that the stone came in in its rough state entailed an extra cost to the purchaser on account of the extra freight on the waste. Surely the fact that the stone is manufactured in Canada; that our stonecutters are being employed by the thousand to cut off that waste, more than compensates this country for the little extra cost of the freight to bring over that stone. It is the old story over again. If we are going to build up an industry in this country, we have to take care of it, and we have not in the past been taking care of the stone quarries or of the stonecutters.
I do not think there is any part of Canada more directly affected by the proposed change in the stone duties than is the province of Manitoba; and it would be a crime, almost, on the part of the Government if they did not do * something at this time to protect that industry. I am strongly in favour of what the minister is trying to do, and I am not at all surprised at the arguments presented by hon. gentlemen on the other side. But I want to tell these gentlemen that while it is all right for those from rural districts like the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) who can make an appeal to the farmers, that hon. gentleman's friends who have to face the labouring men will find it a different proposition.

The Minister of
Finance will recall the fact that in the course of some remarks on a former occasion I called his attention to the representations made by certain quarrying interests. I discharged my obligation to my correspondent in bringing to the notice of the Finance Minister the views of my correspondent. I wish now to supplement what
I stated by reading from another letter. My correspondent, who is a quarryman, says:
The change is entirely in the interest of the stonecutters, or builders, or masons, whatever they may he called-perhaps contractors is the better word. The change gives them the right to import stone sawn on two sides as rough stone, and puts the Canadian quarries completely at the mercy of the contractors. They never import stone sawn on four sides, it is always sawn on two sides if sawn at all and is known as ' mill block.'
This is the representation of a quarryman from the Maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member understand that we have not increased the duty upon rough stone?

I understand that.
The contention I attempted to make was that the change was made in the interest of the contractors, that is, of the men who take contracts to construct a building. It is made easier for them to bring their stone in the form in which they want it- sawn on two sides. In my judgment-only in my judgment, of course-this is not in the interest even of the stonecutter so called, but rather in the interest of the contractor and is against the interest of tihe thousands of quarrymen employed in the stone quarries throughout Canada.
"Mr. WHITE:	That view seems to be
absolutely inconsistent with what we are at all events attempting to do by this legislation, and I cannot conceive how the hon. gentleman arrives at that conclusion.
Because the contractor wants the stone sawn on two sides, he can bring that in more favourably.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I understood the hon. member for West Lambton to say that that was precisely what would not happen- that stone sawn on two sides would not come in now, and that stone would have to be got from Canadian quarries. That is what I had in view when I stated that indirectly it would help the quarrymen.

I am speaking from
the standpoint of the eastern quarrymen. The difficulty with him is to get a market in this section of Canada, because of the high transportation charges. The Indiana and Ohio quarrymen have an advantage over the sandstone quarrymen of eastern Canada by reason of the distance and expense of transportation. There is a dis-

position on the part of contractors in this section of Canada to purchase the stone from Indiana and Ohio. They now get it on payment of 20 per cent duty if it is sawn on not more than two sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is it the hon. member's
opinion that the Government should raise the duty and keep out the stone from Indiana and Ohio?
I am opposed to the raising of all duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then, what is the way
Out?
The hon. minister will pardon me-I am representing for his consideration the views that are presented to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought they were the hon. gentleman's own views.

Not my own views at all. A quarry owner at Montreal writes to me as follows:
You have no doubt observed in Budget speech that it is proposed to protect the stonecutting industry by increasing the duty on manufactured stone, making it 15 cents per 100 pounds on all stone sawn on four sides, and 45 cents per 100 pounds on further manufactured stone. That will prevent the importation of manufactured stone and is evidently worded in the interest of the stonecutting industry only, with the intention of importing stone sawn on two sides only, or unmanufactured. This, of course, would be of no benefit to the stone-quarrying industry of Canada and will not tend toward its development. It shows a very ungenerous disposition on the part of the stone industry and unfairness on the part of the Government towards the stone-quarrying industry of Canada.
The gentleman who wrote this letter is not a supporter of the Liberal party, but a Conservative. These are his views and he honours me with a request to place them before my hon. friend. Now, the point I wish to make is that if the hon. minister is under the impresssion that he he is favouring the man who handles the chisel and ma'let, he is evidently mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is in the mind of my
hon. friend's correspondent-I understand that he has not put this forward as his own view-that the Government should have carried the increase further and placed a higher duty upon rough stone and stone sawn upon two sides? What we have done, as I have stated repeatedly to the committee is to leave the duty as it was. We have not reduced it; we have not increased it; we have left as it was the duty upon rough stone and upon stone sawn upon two sides. I think my hon. friend does not appreciate the fact that a great deal of work is done upon the finished stone; that is the work which we are trying to have done in Canada. We thought that the interests of the consumer would be conserved by allowing stone in the rough and sawn on not more than two sides, to come in under the present rates, and that the further dressing could be done in Canada. I point out to my hon. friend that his correspondent evidently had in mind the idea that the Government should have increased the duty upon stone in the rough and upon stone sawn on two sides.

I have no knowledge of what was in the mind of my correspondent; I have placed on 'Hansard' his views and suggestions, wherein he stated what he did want. I mentioned at the time that I did not endorse his suggestion, but I submitted them for the benefit of my hon. friend and in order to show what a tangle protection places business in. When you take a step towards protecting some particular class of people, you disturb the equilibrium of others; then you have to go back and attempt to restore that equilibrium, thereby occasioning another disturbance.

I recall a discussion which took place in the House a few weeks -ago in which I, as well as the Minister of Public Works, was criticised because in the construction of the public building in the city of Brantford American instead of Canadian stone had been used. The subject was introduced by the hon. member for North Oxford, who has kept a very watchful eye upon the Brantford building. It appears to me that the minister is trying to meet the views of the -hon. member for North Oxford and others who think that Canadian stone

should be used in the construction of Canadian public buildings. I am quite in accordance with that view and I regret
5 p.m. that it was found necessary to use American stone in the construction of the Brantford building. I think the tariff resolution now before the House has in view the doing away with the use of American stone in our Canadian public buildings. The minister is quite consistent when he says that this tariff readjustment is going to improve the quarry industry, and I disagree with the hon. member for Westmorland if he intended to convey the idea that the quairrymen will not be benefited.
I was stating not my own views, but the views of quarrymen as to what they thought the result would be.

I followed the hon. gentleman as closely as possible and I found it very difficult to disentangle his views from those of his correspondent. I am not at all sure whether my hon. friend put any views of his own upon ' Hansard.'
How would this increased duty benefit the quarrymen?

It is evident on the face of it that it will benefit the quarry-men. Heretofore the quarrymen have not had the large machinery for planing the stone on two or four sides, and when the demand for the stone is made sufficiently large and the American stone is kept out when cut on four sides or further manufactured, the result will be the introduction of improved machinery into these smaller quarries, thus enabling the quarrymen to compete with the American manufactured article on even terms. I do not know what quarry the hon. member for Queens, Prince Edward Island, has in view, but I understand that in the province of New Brunswick-in Sackville, for instance-there are quarries which have this improved machinery, which I hope will be further introduced into Canada. I myself think that this Government are laying down the principle that in the construction of any public building to be built of stone, nothing but Canadian stone will be used. It must be evident to hon. gentlemen of the committee that we have ample stone in Canada to erect all our Canadian public buildings, and the use of Canadian etone should be encouraged as much as possible. I believe this resolution of the Minister of Finance will lead to the further
production of Canadian stone; that it will result in the introduction of improved machinery and that stone planed, rounded, and manufactured on four sides will be produced iin Canada instead of in the United States. The quarrymen will be distinctly benefited by this increase of duty on stone to 30 and 45 cents per hundred pounds. 1 want to make it perfectly clear that so far as I am concerned I should like to see Canadian stone used in all our Canadian public buildings. After the imposition of the duty which the Finance Minister is asking us to endorse to-day, I believe that no more buildings will be constructed in Brantford or elsewhere in Canada with American stone, because I believe that Canadian stone can successfully compete with the American product.
In addition to what the Finance Minister has presented, I have been waited on by three or four deputations of stonecutters asking for this very thing, that their in-' dustry be protected. It is a very large industry. I refer to the men who move about and use mallet and chisel. Anybody who watches the progress of a public building will note that these men are very much in evidence upon the ground. So far as the Brantford building is concerned, up to date about $15,000 has been paid to men who have been cutting stone right there on the ground. That is only in one building. What would it be on, all the buildings in Canada if we were to enact legislation that would make it possible for stonecutters to cut all that work upon the ground, to have Canadian and British citizens working upon our own jobs instead of bringing in the stone in a manufactured state from the United States, much of it made by machinery in the very highly specialized quarries of Ohio and Indiana to which the hon. member for Westmorland has referred. I would think that hon. gentleman would be the first to hold up his hands for this duty. I know he would like to help his fellow citizens, but he has the free trade microbe firmly implanted in his brain and he does not think he can stretch a point even to help his own province of New Brunswick in this respect. I venture to say that these correspondents of his and others interested in the stone business in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Quebec and further west as well, all who are engaged in either the quarry business or in stonecutting, will be in full accord with the action of the minister. I think it is a patriotic and national policy with regard to stone

and public edifices which every member on either side should encourage rather than criticise.

I wish to inform my hon. friend that for the last twenty-five or thirty years or even more, they have been sawing stone in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The initiation of that industry in those provinces was at least contemporaneous with the beginning of the sawn stone industry at Berea, and other points in Ohio. I have very great sympathy for the stone quarrying industry but I have a very great sympathy also for all classes of our people; and while the selfishness of the stone quarry men might lead them to ask us to especially pick them out as being entitled to particular favours there is a great consuming class, a building class, the great mass of the people throughout Canada, who perhaps would take a contrary view. The germ to which my hon. friend refers has been for many years in my brain with respect to the matter.

Are very many of
these small houses or cheaper class of buildings made of stone? Are they not usually made of brick or wood?

In our part of Canada wood heretofore has been so very cheap that wooden buildings for residences have prevailed. They can be constructed at a much less cost and we have not so many millionaires although there are a few who live in stone edifices. Many of our public buildings are of stone or of brick.

While 1 appreciate the fact that the minister is putting into effect a very good policy, and that there should be an increase of duty upon stone sawn on four sides, still I think that something should be done for the quarrymen. I would suggest that the duty of fifteen cents should be placed upon rough stone and upon stone sawn on two sides. I believe that if this were done we could develop a stone business in Canada which would fill the requirements of the whole country. To-day the duty of twenty per cent on rough stone is not sufficient. I think that the opinion of all quarrymen in Canada is that twenty per cent on rough stone and on stone sawn on two sides is no protection at all. It may be a benefit to the artisan, to the man engaged in cutting the stone; but will it be a benefit to the quarryman? I think you will find that the opinion of quarrymen all over Canada to-day is that it is no benefit at all. I

have letters similar to that read by the hon. member for Westmorland, saying that the majority of the stone which comes in here to-day is stone sawn on two sides. That will still continue on the old twenty per cent basis, and the manufactured stone, of course, will come under the forty-five cent rate. I do not believe that much of that stone comes into Canada to-day. I do not think that the duty now introduced goes far enough. That is my own opinion and the opinion of gentlemen from whom I have received communications who are engaged in the business. I know that the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Em-merson) is -a free trader ostensibly in certain places. He gave an opinion here as the opinion of a friend of his who was a Liberal-Conservative, but I believe that if he spoke from his own heart he would express the same opinion, perhaps not in this House but to his friends outside.
Order.

The question is not one of free trade against protection, it is a question of a revenue or reasonable tariff against protection. I do not want to be understood as objecting to a reasonable tariff or to the protection that results because of that tariff; but in regard to this item that we have under consideration I think, having listened to the discussion very carefully, that it goes altogether beyond protection and becomes pure piracy. The hon. member from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) has urged that there should be a balance in all these matters as between that which is protected and that at whose expense protection is given. In this ease we have absolutely a minor industry of this country both as to the amount of stone quarried and as to the number of men employed in its quarrying or preparation. Of such a limited character is that industry that everybody knows that all over Canada stone is imported for building purposes. Right here in this city of Ottawa, founded upon a limestone rock, the stone for the largest and latest public buildings-no, I will say the stone for all the later buildings-has been imported. For instance, stone was imported for the Chateau Laurier, the Grand Trunk station, and for a great many office buidings in this city.
Are not all the Canadian buildings built with Canadian stone?

Possibly they were a good while ago, but I am speaking of what is

*occurring to-day or within the last two or three years. The evidence goes to show that for one reason or another this industry is a minor one, and when my hon. friend undertakes to impose such a measure of protection for a minor industry he is simply taxing the public at large for the benefit of a very small proportion of the community. He is placing the many under contribution for the benefit of a very few.

May I he permitted to correct my hon. friend when he makes the statement that all the public buildings in Ottawa recently erected have been built with American stone? The Birks building is of New Brunswick stone.

I did not say all the
buildings. I instanced the Chateau Laurier, the Grand Trunk station, and there are several others, including, I think, the *Carnegie library. The matter is beyond question. We had a debate in this House a short while ago in regard to the imported stone used in the public building at Brantford, and so it is all over the country. We have the case of the building in Regina, cited by my hon. friend from Assiniboia. If it were an important industry that would he benefited in a measurable degree without injury to the public at large, I could see some reason in my hon. friend s making the change; but when he undertakes to burden the community at large ostensibly for the benefit of an industry which is of an essentially minor character, I say that is not protection-it is piracy, and certainly should not form, any part of the policy of a government of this country. There was a tariff on stone before this amendment was brought in. Why was that not a sufficient protection-if you want to call it protection -to those interested in the production of stone, either as quarrymen, builders, or stonecutters. Is it not a fact that stone suitable for building purposes is only found in isolated localities, and that the freight on that stone to the place where it is used is equal in, large measure to the actual cost of production? That is to say, the freight is in all cases a large part of the total cost of the stone; therefore, stone situated near where it is going to be used enjoys an advantage, by reason of the freight rate, that with the duty formerly prevailing should be sufficient encouragement and protection to that industry. My hon. friend has mentioned conditions in the West. My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) mentioned that in his constituency there
are a large number of quarries-and that is true. But from there to the Rocky mountains there are 800 miles of territory where there is actually not one quarry or the possibility of one, but where there is the certainty of there being from day to day and for all time to come an enormous demand for building material. Does my hon. friend think it right that that vast area of country should be compelled to contribute to the industry that is located in his particular constituency? Does he think that is fair? Does he think that is the National Policy? It is a Selkirk policy, but it is not even a western policy.
What about the policy you voted for last night?
Never mind about that. In what way does my hon. friend object to my vote of last night?
It was a more selfish -polieyT-so-tar as the-National Rolicyms con- oerned, than this, and if it had been carried into effect it would have affected detrimentally farmers all over the country.

I voted for it because I
believed it would have affected beneficially the farmers of my part of the country and of my hon. friend's part of the country.
It would have ruined hundreds of people in my constituency.

Not one. It would have been of benefit to the farmers of my hon. friend's constituency and to the farmers of my own constituency. While on this point, let me say that the vote was a vote to allow the farmer to sell his potatoes where he could find a market for them. My hon. friend from Selkirk to-day is standing up in this House to say that the man who wants to build a good building in the prairie provinces shall not have the privilege of doing it unless he pays an unjust toll to the quarrymen in the constituency of Selkirk or in some other part of the country. That is the difference between the two policies. I say that it goes hard with the men who are refused the privilege of selling their products in the open market to be compelled to buy what they require under the high tariff that the minister sees fit to impose. He has said to-day that it is his purpose to compel them to do 30.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To do what?
To compel those who want to use good stone to pay the price that the quarrymen and stonecutters of Canada see fit to ask.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How many farmers in the Northwest will use cut stone on their buildings?

The farmers of the Northwest will not use cut stone in their buildings; that is a certainty. More than that, I can tell my hon. friend that unless con-t ditions in the West are changed-as he could change them by a change of policy- the farmers in the Northwest will not be able to build many buildings for many years to come. But there axe other people in the Northwest besides the farmers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it not chiefly the large corporations, banks, railway companies and such like, that use cut stone; the Chateau Laurier for example?

My hon. friend and I are quite in agreement. I have told him that the farmers are not going to use cut stone; they are not even using lumber just now, as his lumber friends will tell him. But there are towns and cities throughout the Northwest which are using cut stone when they can get it at a reasonable price. It is the hope and ambition of the people of every little town, and of every big town too, in the West, to erect handsome buildings, good public buildings, and good private buildings. They desire to use cut stone, so far -a.s possible, in the beautifying of those buildings; and at this particular time when times are harder than they have been for years my hon friend comes forward with a proposition that-as he has repeatedly declared to-day, and everybody knows it-will lay an abnormal tax on the use of cut -stone. My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee) says it will be a prohibitive tax. I ask my hon. friend if I am not justified in using the expressions I have.
