speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not by any means.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why cannot they have that ornamentation and why cannot the cutting of stone take place in Canada? I am admitting the rough stone at the same rate as before. Why cannot stonecutting industries be developed in Calgary, Regina and a number of other places to supply the needs of the West?

Can my hon. friend explain why the cut stone industry has not been established there long ago? The stone is there, the demand has been there but we have been importing -cut stone from the United States. If the people in the quarry and stone industry have not made provision for meeting the demand in Canada, that is their fault and not ours, and we should not be punished for it. But my hon. friend is going to punish us because the men who own the quarries have not been as enterprising as he thinks they ought to have been. In so far as the consumer is concerned at any rate, my hon. friend undertakes to tie up the whole of the western country and to hand it over to a small number of quarrymen, contractors and stonecutters in order to prevent the erection and beautification of buildings throughout the whole western country.
My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) said a few moments ago that this would not ultimately redound to the benefit of the stonecutters-. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance did not see- fit to take up the matter as my hon. friend from A-ssiniboia had stated it. My hon. friend from Assiniboia -stated, and he stated what was absolutely true, that the increase in the tax on cut stone will prevent the use of -cut stone. My hon. friend from- Lambton (Mr. Pardee) has given figures which show that the rate is prohibitory under this new tariff. I ask then, if the use of cut stone is going to be prohibited by my hon. friend's tariff, how is the- stonecutter going to get employment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will not be prohibitive.

My hon. friend did not contradict the figures of my hon. friend from Lambton, and certainly the figures declare that it is prohibitory. A few minutes ago the hon. member for North

Essex (Mr. Wilcox) told the committee that the Government was. erecting a building in Walkerville, and was trimming that building with Roman stone-cement blocks -instead of with good cut stone. Are the stonecutters going to get any work out of that, I would ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance? If he puts on this imposition so that men cannot use cut stone and are compelled to do without ornamentation or use cement, where is the stonecutter being benefited by the proposal that he makes? My hon. friend has introduced a proposition that he thought some political capital was to be got out of upon the plea that it was going to furnish work for stonecutters. It is not only not going to furnish work for stonecutters, hut he is going to do a great and lamentable injury, certainly to the prairie provinces, whatever may be the result iu other parts of the country. My hon. friend seems to be very extreme on the question of protection. All that anybody has to do is to come to him with a suggestibiT for the~im-position of taxation on the people of Canada, or of an increase of existing taxation, and forthwith it is imposed or increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
There may be others-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are others.

There may be people who have thought of things that my hon. friend has not acceded to, hut the list of things that he has acceded to is sufficiently startling, and there is none more inexcusable than the imposition of an increased duty on cut stone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) appears, as usual, to misunderstand this question. But before I deal with the matter on its merits, in answer to my hon. friend, I desire to call attention to a new theory in economics put forward by the hon. gentleman, which I think merits the attention of the committee. He said that if you had a large, or a major, industry, it would be a proper case for an increase of the tariff.
I did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend suggested that without question.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend said that
if you had a large industry there might be something said for a tariff increase.
I said that I could see the reason that my hon. friend would put forward.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All right, let us say that
my hon. friend could see it in connection with a large, or major, industry, which industry,- being well established, in all probability does not need the assistance of a protective tariff. He says that it is statesmanship in the case of a large industry, but in the case of a minor industry he says it is piracy-statesmanship on the one hand in connection with a large industry that does not need protection, whereas, in the case of the minor industry, it is piracy.
Sure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
How long will the stonemit.tt.ing industry of Canada_remain__a
minor industry unless we change this tariff? It will continue to remain a minor industry, but if we give this moderate tariff increase, this reasonable degree of protection, there is every prospect of this minor industry becoming a major industry. My hon. friend talked about this tariff change being prohibitory and about the people of the West and other parts of Canada being deprived of the privilege of using cut stone. My hon. friend has failed to understand the changes which the Government proposes. My hon. friend should know that any stone-cutting industry in the West can bring in rough stone and stone sawn on two sides at precisely the same rate as was approved by the Goverment of which he was a member. The tariff has not been increased in respect to stone in the rough and it can be brought from the United States .or any other country. What we are seeking to do is to have that stone finished and further manufactured in Canada, and we believe that this change will have the effect of building up the stone-cutting industry and, by indirection, I believe, although that view is not concurred in by some gentlemen on my own side of the House, it will have the effect of assisting in the development of the stone quarries of Can-da. I feel that I am on safe ground this afternoon for several Teasons. In the first place, I am sure of the facts myself, and in the second place, we have had a great

diversity of view on the other side of the House. We have had one hon. member contending that there should be no tariff upon stone, another, that the proposed changes should not be made, and some others on my own side, and I think one, by suggestion, at all events, upon the other side, putting forward the view that the tariff increases had not gone far enough and that they 'should be extended so as to give further protection to the quarry industry. I have adopted the middle course, the course which, I think, should recommend itself to this committee, and I therefore submit that this tariff change is reasonable and neither extreme nor prohibitive. An average duty of thirty per cent can not be regarded, under the conditions that exist in Canada to-day, as prohibitive. If my hon. friend will look at the tariff which he approved when he was a member of the late Government, he will find that thirty per cent was not regarded as a prohibitive rate. Why should he now say that it is a prohibitive rate? I absolutely deny that it is prohibitive.
Is there not a vast difference between thirty per cent on stone and thirty per cent, say, on cotton?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the tariff goes, thirty per cent is not a prohibitive rate, and this will not have the effect of prohibiting the use of cut stone in Canada. It ought, as a matter of fact, rather to increase the use of cut stone in Canada by building up stonecutting industries here.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have had several applications from iron and steel manufacturers, not for any specific form of assistance, but to take some tariff action that would be of advantage to the industry. If my hon. friend will-as I have no doubt he has- look over the legislation which I am bringing down now he will find that there are many changes which will inure to the advantage of the industry. But as to the ground upon which we refused to renew the bounties to the steel industries-which I understand to be his question-I may say that no application has been before the Government for a continuance of the bounties upon iron and steel during the past year or two. The more recent applications have been along the line of placing a tariff upon wire rods and taking authority to the Governor in Council to increase the duty on structural iron and steel of the heavier weights rather than for a renewal of bounties. I said in my Budget Speech, and I say now to the hon. gentleman, because he was not present on that occasion, that while I know there is a difference of opinion among members of this House and among the public with respect to the propriety of



granting bounties, my own opinion is that bounties are justifiable in certain cases. Capital is always timid. There are always risks in connection with the establishment of a large new industry. In the case of the iron industry, as the hon. gentleman knows, each one presents its own problems, and it may be that even the best-conceived scheme will encounter vicissitudes of fortune in its early years causing capital to undergo very serious risks. The result is that capital is timid about embarking upon large new enterprises unless there is some Government assistance. My view is that the Government is justified in granting bounties in proper cases for the purpose of calling industries into beingwhichotherwi-e would not be started or which might be delayed in establishment for many years. Consequently, I have never seen any reason to disagree with the policy of the late Government in granting bounties to call into existence the *steel industry at Sydney. There are differences of opinion, as I say, but I am giving my own view. But after an industry has been established, and has enjoyed for many years the advantage of bounties, I think at should be allowed to stand upon its own basis. It would be evidence to mo that the bounties had failed of effect if, after having been enjoyed for many years by an industry which has advantages in the way of raw material which would put it upon a par with similar industries in any part of the world, a continuance of tho bounties' should be required. If any assistance were required for such an industry I would rather give it by means of a tariff change. To more particularly answer my hon,. friend, the question of continuance or renewal of bounties has not been actively before the Government for some considerable time.

I think I can explain
best by stating the present position. My hon. friend knows that to-day coke is on the free list for all purposes. manufacturers-and to foundrymen engaged in the melting of metals. Under the present tariff it is not possible for a Canadian manufacturer of coke to obtain the drawback upon the bituminous coal which he imports to be used in the manufacture of his product, if he sells that product to a foundryman engaged in business next door or in some adjacent town. That seems an anomaly, and the matter was drawn especially to our attention by the proposed establishment of a coke industry in Hamilton. If, on the other hand, a drawback would be allowed-which it was represented to us would not in any way adversely affect the coal industry of Canada-in which I know my hon. friend from Pietou takes a special interest-the plant would be established in Hamilton. I looked into the. question and I found that the Canadian manufacturer, speaking generally, is at a disadvantage compared with his American competitor so far as freight rates are concerned. In other words, the International Harvester Company would not maintain itself in the city of Hamilton in the manufacture of agricultural implements at a cost in 'excess of what it could manufacture for in Chicago if the Canadian market were open to it equally with the market of the United States.

We have reached the conclusion that the apprehension on the part of the nail-making firms who have opposed the granting of a duty is not well founded. We believe it is in the interest of the nail-making industry as well as the wire rod industry that a duty should be imposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There can be no object on the part of the manufacturers of wire rods, who would desire to increase their product and find a market for it in Canada, attempting to destroy those industries engaged in the manufacture of nails. They have expressly repudiated any intention of doing so and it has been my own experience that these large concerns do not deliberately set about trying to injure smaller concerns. The object of the manufacturers of wire rods-the Dominion Iron and Steel Companies and Steel Company of Hamilton, who are engaged in the manufacture' of wire rods-is to sell their product to those engaged in the manufacture of nails and it is inconceivable that they should attempt to destroy them. My hon. friend will admit, I am sure, that those who have a protection at the present time of.60 cents per keg upon wire nails can hardly be heard to object to the imposition of a reasonable duty on wire rods. Wire rods, as my hon. friend knows, have been upon the free list. We have placed a duty of $3.50, general, upon wire rods when imported for us in making wire into coil in the importers' own factories. That is a duty under 15 per cent and it did not appear to me, after his having given the matter as careful and painstaking consideration as I have ever given any question in my life, that it would be just to deny to the manufacturers of wire rods a duty as reasonable as that by reason of the fact that the manufacturer of nails, having a duty of 60 cents a keg, wjiich would represent probably 30 per cent or more-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When I used those words, I used them generally, not speaking of the manufacture of wire rods only; but I have held the view that the manufacturers in Canada of any commodity, enjoying the benefits of the protective system, should endeavour to take care of their market, and should not pursue any course having as its object the destruction of other enterprises. In other words, I believe that they should carry on their business in a fair way. What is a fair way will depend upon circumstances and upon the judgment that is brought to bear upon the matter. I realise the difficulties of the Government undertaking to pronounce upon what is fair and what is unfair, but I would not hesitate to say that if I came to the conclusion that a deliberate course was being pursued-and no such circumstances have been brought to my attention since I have been a minister-of attempting to destroy or injure others who were endeavouring to carry on their business in a proper way in Canada, I would not hesitate to pass an Order in Council reducing or even abolishing the duty. Take the case of the cement cut; I held, and I said, too, in this House, that it was the duty of the cement manufacturers to take care of their market and to provide that, when the West wanted cement as they knew they would want cement, that cement should be at the head of the lakes in time to meet the requirements of the West. Having failed to do that in that particular year, I had no hesitation in reaching the conclusion that I should cut the duty in half for a limited period. In this case I do not hold out any threat, because I do not think any threat is necessary. I believe that it is in the interest of the manufacturers of wire rods to carry on their business fairly with the manufacturers of wire nails. I have no reason to believe that they will take any undue or improper advantage of this tariff imposition, which I believe is clearly necessary if we are to have a wire rod industry in Canada. Personally, I do not like to look forward to the possibility of this country having to depend absolutely upon a supply of wire rods from external sources.

The large companies have assured the minister
That they will, by no means, injure those engaged in the nail business.
I did not know but that the minister might be able to give us some idea as to how they will be able to operate this busi-
ness without injuring small nail-makers. In my judgment, the minister is creating a monopoly in the hands of two great companies that may jump the price of Wire rods to the small nail men and then jump the price of nails to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend aware that I have not raised the duty on nails?

Yes, I am aware that the minister has not raised the duty on nails. If he had lowered the duty on nails he might have been able to protect the consumer, but instead of that he leaves the duty where it is, equal to about 40 per cent of the present value f.o.b. Pittsburg. The rate is 60 cents per keg, and the effect will be that by this duty of 174 cents upon wire rods, the minister will take three-quarters of a million dollars out of the pockets of the people on the one item of nails, which are the product of wire rods. These two companies will not injure the small nail makers, tout they will charge the small nail-makers 17J cents more for their rods and then they will make the price that they will charge the wholesale trade, and I venture to say that you will find that nails when sold to the consumer will be at least fifty cents a keg higher than they were last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman if the price of nails has fallen in the last two years, and if so, how much?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much?

I think about 20 cents
per keg.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the building trade resume its activity if they went up 20 cents a keg?

I do not know that I
would be very much surprised if they went up 50 cents a keg; that is what I expect to see.
Mr. "WHITE: How much of the duty of 60 cents a keg is now taken by the manufacturer of nails in Canada?

Nearly the whole of it
is taken. The base price of nails in Canada is about $1.90 and the base price in Pittsburg is about $1.40, so that a large proportion of the duty of 60 cents per keg on nails is now added to the price by the Canadian manufacturers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to ask my
hon. friend how the price by any chance could go up 50 cents a keg if there is only 20 cents of a leeway under the tariff?

There will (be a perfect
monopoly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not raising the duty on nails.

I admit you are not raising the duty on nails; but the effect will be that, when the 171 cents aTe added to the price of the raw material, notwithstanding the promise that the small nail manufacturers are not to be hurt, the two large mills that supply the wire rods to the small mills will be able to dictate prices. The small mills will make as much money as they make now and perhaps more. Possibly they are unduly competing one with another at the present time, and that is perhaps one reason why nails are being sold now at a reasonable price. The wholesale price at present, I think, is $2.10 to $2.15; but the Pender people in St. John and the Maritime people were selling them as low or a little lower than $2 base, but at present the-price in Montreal is $2.15 in a small way. I may be wrong, but my judgment is that the minister is placing this industry of manufacturing nails in the hands of two great steel companies, the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and the Steel Company of Hamilton, who together manufacture 70 per cent of the 1,500,000 kegs used in Canada which amounts to 1,050,000 kegs, so that they can very well afford to accept 171 cents per 100 lb. extra from the small companies when they have the power to dictate to the small companies what shall be the price of nails to the wholesale trade. As the hon. minister goes around the country in his automobile-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not got one.

and when he sees the farmers using four or five kegs of nails in the construction of a barn, he will see that he is taking out of the consumers an extra tax of $2.50 for the construction of each barn, because of this duty. It would not be so bad if he could limit it to 171 cents per 100 lb., the amount of the duty on the rods. There is no difficulty for a number of nail manufacturers to form a combine; but they *sometimes (become dissatisfied one with another, and the combine is not maintained. That has occurred recently. But owing to the control by the two large companies, I suggest that the small companies will be
subject to their dictation as to the price at which the nails are to be sold to the trade.
Is the price necessarily raised to the consumer? [DOT]

That has been our experience. You cannot have a monopoly where there is not a large investment; but whenever you have a large investment in say two companies, there can easily be arranged a monopoly as to selling price.

Has the minister not
provided against that?
No, he has not provided. He has put into the hands of the Dominiou Iron and Steel Company and the Steel Company of Hamilton the power to chaTge what prices they can.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Apart from the tariff of sixty cents per one hundred pounds on nails, which I have not changed, what was to prevent the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and the Steel Company of Hamilton and the small nail manufacturers from getting together, because that is what my hon. friend suggested last summer? What change is there in that regard? My hon. friend says that will create a monopoly in the manufacture of nails. What was to hinder them from doing that last year? My hon. friend knows that I have not changed the duty on nails.	.
That is exactly what was done. The prices went up but the monopoly did not stand. The agreement was not adhered to by each of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was under the present tariff?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was not responsible for
that.
But you are now confining the monopoly to two companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The others are still in
business.

The others cannot move
because they are dictated to by the wire companies that supply the wire rods. They will dictate to the people of Canada and take out of their pockets $750,000 because fifty cents a keg on 1,500,000 kegs is equal to $750,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon friend comes from the Maritime provinces; and apart from the particular intelligence that characterizes all who come from there, they are all interest-

ed in the steel industry. The steel industry is one of the great basic industries of Canada, and I think it is a mistake to look upon these two companies simply as two companies, for we must remember that they represent a great deal of capital, including English and foreign capital. Does my hon. friend think it fair that under our system those two great industries should not have a reasonable measure of protection on their wire rod production, which is,one of the most important branches of their production? Under present conditions, and especially under the conditions which prevail in the United States to-day, that powerful corporation, the United States Steel Company, highly specialized, developed over very many years under a protective system, is able to hold its own market and to sell its wire rods in Canada at two or three dollars a ton below the cost of production, let us say, at Hamilton. I have had the matter looked into, and I know the cost in the city of Hamilton to the Steel Company of Hamilton. My hon. friend, as I understand him. is opposed to the imposition of a duty upon wire rods.

I have not so much objection to the duty on wire rods as I have to your allowing to remain a duty of 60 cents per keg on nails. If you would reduce the duty on nails, you would prevent and avoid the difficulty of a combine and an undue advance in the price of the manufactured article.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is usually a very fair minded man. Does he not think he would get the manufacture of nails coming and going? Under the Fielding tariff, under which my hon. friend sat for many years, and to which, I believe, he gave very generous and loyal support, for which I do not blame him, the duty on nails was 60 cents per keg, and the wire rods from which those nails were made were on the free list. I have raised the duty on wire rods to $3.50 per ton, and my hon. friend does not dissent from my action. What about the manufacture of wire nails? Under the Fielding tariff he had 60 cents per keg protection, equal to from 30 per cent to 40 per cent, and he had his wire rods free. I raised his wire rods to $3.50; and my hon. friend, who never protested before, so far as I can learn, against the duty of '60 cents per keg imposed by the late Government, says now that it is an injustice ttf' tv* consuming

public because we do not reduce the duty . upon wire nails. If we did that, as I said, we would get the manufacturer coming and going. We would increase the cost of his raw material, and we would decrease the protection, which presumably has been reasonable, because it was supported by my reasonable friend (Mr. Loggie), I think my hon. friend's apprehensions are not well founded, and I will tell him why. There is a competition in the country in respect of nails, and I do not believe a combine will be formed because it is too big a country. At the present time the nail manufacturers of Canada are not taking advantage of the full amount of the tariff rates. It is often stated in this House that the price of an article in Canada is determined by the cost of production plus the freight and the duty. That is not correct. It may be correct in some cases; but it is by no means correct in all cases, and it certainly is not correct in the case of nails.
How much of that tariff do the nail manufacturers pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the present time I am not in agreement with my hon. friend, although he may be correct. I will make this statement, that they are not taking anything like the whole of the tariff protection.
They are not taking any of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to have my hon. friend, who is engaged in the business, make that statement. I understood they were either taking none or very little of the protection. In Canada we have an over-production of nails, which one would expect in a period like this; when there has been somewhat of a stagnation in building activities one would expect that the price of nails would fall. I have been advised, as my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) states, that the nail manufacturers are not taking any of the duty. Assuming that what my hon. friend (Mr. Loggie) states is correct, that is that they are taking a little more than half of the duty, the balance is leeway for them to go upon if they desire to take advantage of the protection afforded by the tariff rates. I do not suggest for a moment that should be done, because I think the price should be determined by competition in Canada within the tariff wall. And the safeguard against monopoly is the power of the Government to reduce the rates upon wire nails or other commodities in the

event of a combine being formed, and there is the necessary legislation on the statute book already to enable the Government to take that action.

I quite appreciate the
fear expressed by my hon. friends on this side. There is no monopoly at present; I understand some of the manufacturers are selling wire nails at less than cost. But when the Dominion Steel Company and the Canada Steel Company have the benefit of these duties on rods, as they manufacture nails also, it is possible that they will say to the other manufacturers of nails: We will sell your rods at a certain price, but if we catch you cutting the price of nails we will sell you no more rods. I am not a prophet, nor am I a prophet's son, so I am not going to say that that is what they will do. But they cannot do it now, because the rods come in free, and the smaller manufacturers can laugh at the big concerns and even compete with them. As to the help that this duty will give, I hope it will be as useful as my hon. friends thinks it will. My own notion is that both these concerns should be reorganized from the inside. I have said that before.

I desire to correct a wrong impression of my hon. friend when he spoke of the prices of nails in the United States and Canada. At present in the United States there are three large concerns that in the past twenty months have gone into the manufacture of nails-the Jones and Loughlon Company, of Pittsburg; the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company, of Youngstown, Ohio; and the Cambria Company, of Johnstown, Pa. Prices are unduly depressed in the United States. I have here the Iron Age, which gives the price of nails in Chicago as $1.78. Nails are selling to-day in Toronto and Hamilton at $1.85. During my connection with the business, which extends over eight or nine years, 1 have never seen nails selling in Canada at higher prices than they were selling for in Chicago. Now, as a matter of fact, no person can buy wire rods in the United States cheaper than $24.50 per ton. If you take the cost of conversion, which is $15 per ton, from the cost per ton of the wire nails as sold at $1.78, you will find that wire rods for conversion purposes are estimated by these concerns at $20 per ton.
Now, as to the matter of wire nails, there is no possibility of combination.
10	p.m. The American market for the finished product is so low as 199
compared with the raw material, and the rate at which they can send them in here is so low that nails must always be sold at a very narrow margin in Canada. I do not think there is a possibility of anybody suffering through the imposition of this duty. Tremendous competition is an economic waste. Some makers may be better situated than others for getting raw material, and when there is a free market, they compete unduly, lake, for instance, the makers in New Brunswick. The man who manufactures wire in New Brunswick can bring in his raw material into St. John cheaper than can any manufacturer in the West, and at the same time, he can land his product in Winnipeg and the West, for virtually the same amount as can any manufacturer in Ontario.
So far as the manufacture of nails is concerned, I am sure that any change will be a change for the better. The companies are all confronted with the fact that the United States Steel Corporation is coming over shortly and will manufacture all lines of wire products and steel. They will supply themselves with semi-raw material on which they will take all the profit on the other side and will sell here in competition on that basis. Just as the American manufacturers of reapers do. They have branches here and they send in material from the United States semi-finished, they assemble it here and sell. There is no method of getting at such concerns for dumping, and there will be ample and free competition in Canada.
Now, as to whether anybody is going to suffer, whether anybody is going to be placed in the hands of the large corporations, I would remind the committee that the minister in his speech stated that if there was any attempt to squeeze the small manufacturer, the Government would take prompt action and put a stop to it. I do not think any Minister of the Crown has ever made that statement before in the case of an industry of this kind. In view of that statement, I think it would be well for us to accept the situation. For we must all recognize that if we are going to get the wider markets which my hon. friends from the West talk about, we must increase the number of workingmen in this country. The United States, in 1872, discovered that the state of Illinois was producing such large quantities of wheat that their surplus was more than ample to supply all the requirements of the British market. And a great panic ensued, the people fearing that they could not find a

market. The Americans took that into consideration and increased their duty on everything, adopting a higher protective
policy. They went on this basis:	If a man
in England -is producing goods for the United States, only about ten per cent ot the flour he consumes would be produced in the United States, And in our case today, if a man in the United States produces an article to be sent to Canada, on y about one-tenth of one per cent of the food he consumes is produced in Canada. me remedy, of course, is to put up a tariff wall and have these men produce goods here. In that way the western farmer will get the benefit of the whole consumption of these people. And in the United States, by putting up that wall, they are enabled to consume virtually all the food they produce, except in some years when they have an exceptional margin of wheat, but are never in danger of suflering because of the need
of a wider market
The best place to get a wider market i? right here in this country; Canada is suffering at the present time from too much importation. Many of our friends in the West, if given the choice between an American! made and a Canadian made article, buy the American article. It does seem to me that the proper way to look at this matter is from the national standpoint; from the standpoint of what is going to benefit the country the most and of what is going to benefit the farmers in the West the most. How are they going to get their wider market? Every man who supplies goods to the people of this country should be compelled to live in Canada, so that he will help consume the grain of the West. Where are all these new cities going to get their woTkingmen? How are they going to exist unless the Government of this country wisely places a tariff upon certain articles and encourages their manufacture in this country? I heard a protest from hon. gentlemen. from the West this afternoon with regard to quarry stone. A quarry employing 200 men is in operation a few miles this side of Winnipeg. Why should not all this stone be manufactured in Canada? I had some work to do in my riding on a public building, and I insisted that a large quantity of Canadian marble should he used in its construction. The result was that there was opened at Maddock a fine quarry that will supply millions of dollars worth of fine marble stone which might otherwise be brought all the way from Ttaly. Is it not 
better to have the workingmen of this country, who consume the beef and grain of the West, polish and manufacture this marble than to have it done by foreign workmen who consume only a very small proportion of the products of our farms? It is just as essential for us to have a large number of factories in this country and to have workingmen consuming our products as it is for the United States-and the example of the United States is a very good example to follow. I do not think anybody will suffer from this duty on wire rods; I do not think that the smaller people will be put out of business. I have an interest in a mill and if it were not beneficial I would be the first man to denounce it.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend that the duty will not hurt the small mill, but I fear the dictation of prices all over Canada. Why can we not in Canada manufacture rods into nails as cheaply as they can in the United States?
Does my hon. friend not think that the Canadian manufacturer is entitled to a fair and reasonable profit, or must he do business for nothing?

Is it not a fair assumption that the United States manufacturer of nails makes a profit? Assuming that the rods cost the American manufacturer $24.50 a ton and the Canadian manufacturer $28 a ton, why should there be any greater difference between the prices of the manufactured article than the difference between the respective costs of the raw material? I have handled thousands of kegs of nails, and I have never in my life handled any other than Canadian nails for consumption in Canada.

Have yon ever made
any money on them?

I certainly have. I have bought United States nails in the United States for consumption in that country, and I have often wondered why there should be so much difference between the price in Canada and the price in the United States.

I told the hon. gentleman a moment ago that if the American manufacturers had to pay for their rods the price at which they are willing to sell them, $24.50, it would be impossible for them to sell nails at $1.75 a keg. But the American	concerns have a

great many improved processes of manufacture. The larger concerns across the line own their own ore and their own coal and manufacture their own pig iron and steel, and they are willing to forego the profits on ten operations perhaps in order to make a profit upon one. I have never known the manufacturers of this country to sell nails at a price one cent higher than they were selling in Chicago, and I think that if the Canadians can get their nails as cheaply in Canada as they are selling in Chicago, nobody need worry.
If the Canadian can get his nails at the same price as the American, plus the amount of the duty we are placing upon the rods, I shall make no complaint whatever.

The Canadian manufacturer cannot get his labour nearly as cheaply as it is obtained in the big iron centres of the United States. The labour employed in this business is largely col oured and foreign labour, Poles and Bulgarians. They are paid $1.25 a day, whereas we pay labourers $2 a day.

I understand
that there is a provision in the resolution whereby the new tariff applicable to wire rods shall not become operative until July next. If that is the case, will the minister explain why that provision has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolution 6 is as follows:
6. Resolved, that the foregoing provisions shall he held to have come into force on the seventh day of April, 1914, and to have applied to all goods imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that day, and to have also applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day, except as otherwise provided in the foregoing resolutions:
Provided, notwithstanding any increase in Customs under the said resolutions, that all goods actually purchased on or before the sixth day of April, 1914, for importation into Canada, on evidence satisfactory to the Minister of Customs of the purchase having been so made, and all goods in warehouse in Canada on such day, if entered for duty after importation prior to the first day of July, 1914, may be entered at the rate of duty in force on the said sixth day of April, 1914.
The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), referring to that proviso said it was unprecedented. That is not the fact and I privately drew his attention to it after his speech. In 1904, upon what was regarded, as I regard this, as a partial revision of the tariff, a similar provision 1991
was attached to the tariff resolutions. I shall read the resolution of that day:
6. Resolved, that the foregoing provision shall be held to have come into force on the eighth day of June, 1904, and to have applied to all goods imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that day, and to have also applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day, except as otherwise provided in the foregoing resolutions: Provided, that all goods actually purchased on or before the seventh day of June, 1904, at any place out of Canada, for importation into Canada, on evidence to the satisfaction of the Minister of Customs of the purchase having been so made, and all goods in warehouse in Canada on such day, may be entered for duty at the rate of duty in force immediately before the said day (without special duty) ; notwithstanding any increase in Customs duties under the said resolutions, but this proviso shall cease to have force and effect after the thirty-first day of August in the present year.
That was the resolution in 1904 applying to the tariff changes made at that time. I made inquiry about this matter and I think this was the reason that the proviso of 1904 was introduced just as is the reason for the proviso to-day: When a general revision of the tariff is being effected the people are aware that such revision is to be made and in consequence it is not usual to allow a time within which goods in respect of which contracts have been entered into for purchase shall be admitted; but in the ease of such an extensive revision as, while not a general revision, is regarded as a partial revision of the tariff it is only fair that parties who have engaged to purchase goods, having had no notice that the partial revision was in contemplation, should be given a reasonable time within which to import at the existing rates goods which they had previously contracted to purchase. That is the reason why this proviso has been attached to the tariff resolution. It would seem to me manifestly unjust that in the case of a revision so extensive as this is men should be penalized by having to pay increased rates of duty in respect of goods they had ordered with delivery extending over a considerable period in the future, without having any notice that the revision was in contemplation.

There has been a long
discussion of wire nails. I understand that there are a number of factories apart from nail manufactories using wire rods. Would the minister give a statement of the industries of which wire rods are the raw material?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Wire rods are the basis of wire products of all kinds including wire

nails. The manufacturers of wire draw their wire from the wire rods and would be affected in this that their raw material is now dutiable to the extent of $3.50 per ton. Of course, my hon. friend knows that they have the benefit of a protective tariff so far as their industry is concerned and tny hon. friend also knows that I have given a drawback in respect of the duty on wire rods entering into the production of wire used for wire fencing. I did that because I thought that the agriculturist of Canada was interested in the price of wire fencing and I therefore, gave the drawback of 99 per cent in respect of wire rod entering into the production of wire of 9, 12 and 13 gauge which is used in the manufacture of fencing. I have dealt with wire and with wire rods. My hon. friend was not in the House when I dealt with the other tariff item, with chains.

speechtext: I will explain that to my hon. friend. As the item does not appear, some explanation is necessary before my hon. friend or any one else can understand it. An Order in Council was passed on the 11th August, 1908, placing brass upon the free list, as brass was not then manufactured in Canada. Can they meet the demands of the country F

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that they can. After making very careful inquiries we are convinced that no objection will be put forward by those who use brass as their raw material, to this restoration of brass to the old 10 per cent item in the tariff. The history of it is that in the tariff revision of 1907 it was in-

tended that all fishing twine should be placed on the free list, but by some mistake unbarked marlin was not referred to in item 682 of the tariff which deals with the matter. It was announced toy the Minister of Finance on that occasion that fishing twine was to be free. It was discovered later on that unbarked marlin was omitted. This discovery was not really made until two or three years ago and for a number of years after the last revision of the tariff this particular kind of twine was admitted free in the customs houses of Nova Scotia. When the present Government came into power a circular was sent out by the Minister of Customs warning the customs officers against admitting this twine free any longer. The consequence was that a duty of 25 per cent was levied upon this twine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that the present Government rendered a decision in this matter that was not in force before?

Yes, practically that.
I drew the matter to the attention of the Government in the session of 1912, and the minister will find in the discussion a copy of the notice that was sent out by the Commissioner of Customs notifying the customs houses to levy this 25 per cent duty upon this particular kind of twine. As a matter of fact, the first notice that was sent out was an instruction to levy on both kinds of twine used in the lobster fishery, but that was afterwards corrected and it was then confined to what is known as unbarked marlin. Right or wrong, this twine had been admitted free until these instructions went out subsequent to the advent of the present Government to power.
I thought I would only have to draw the matter to the attention of the Government to have it adjusted, and I have done so on several occasions. The last time, in February of this year, I had the assurance of the Minister of Customs that when the tariff was dealt with this matter would be attended to. It was not attended to, and when the Budget came down I made an inquiry and the minister on that occasion stated that there was some difficulty about it, but he did not explain very fully what the difficulty was.
I note that in these items that we are dealing with at the present time the minister is generous to the manufacturers, but (Mr. Sinclair.]
he does not seem to have the same interest in the fishermen. For example, 533a:
Garnetted wool waste in the white when imported by manufacturers of woollen goods for use exclusively in their own factories
is free. The next item:
Jute or hemp yarn, plain, dyed or coloured, when imported by manufacturers for use exclusively in their own factories for weaving purposes, or for insulating wire, or for the manufacture of hammocks and twines
is free. The next item, 543
Linen yarn when imported by manufacturers of towels, damask, or seamless linen fire hose duck, for use exclusively in the manufacture of such articles in their own factories
is free. If there is a reason for refusing the request of 65,000 fishermen on the coast of the Maritime provinces I would like to know what it is. In this discussion it has come out on more than one occasion that changes have been made and duties imposed at the instance of one small factory. Last night it was disclosed that a small firm of Yankees at Port Hope had influence enough with this Government to get their raw material placed on the free list. Another small firm at Windsor had influence enough to impose a tax on caustic soda which is used by the soap manufacturers of this country and which will affect every man who uses soap and we all do on this side of the House. How does it come that the fishermen have not any influence with this Government?
They do not use the right kind of bait.

I think that some little concession is due to the fishermen of this country. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) promised them free medicine although he seems to have forgotten all about it. The free twine I am asking for now is only a bagatelle compared with the expense of providing free medicine and free medical attendance for the 65,000 fishermen on the coast of eastern Canada. In my own constituency the fishermen and farmers have been turned down in every request they have made to the present Government. The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) cancelled all the appropriations by the late Government for the building of breakwaters and improvements along the coast of the county I represent. He cancelled them after they had been voted and after tenders had been asked and contracts made in some cases. When I asked him why he did it he

said that he had other more important places to attend to. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) cancelled a contract to build a branch line in my constituency and he did not stop there. He imposed a higher rate of freight on fresh fish and now the men who are engaged in the fishing industry have to struggle against that difficulty. If they want to send a carload of fish to the market they have to pay $10 or $12 more than they had to pay in 1911. The hon. Minister of Tirade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) when we asked him if he would consider an application from the fishermen along the coast for better communication with the Boston market so that they could get the advantage of the big prices that are going there for their fresh fish hardened his heart too and would not listen to our request. I thought I would have better luck with the Minister of Finance. I thought I was approaching a man who take3 a broader view and does not allow questions of. petty politics to enter into the consideration at all. I was depending upon him to do something and I must say that if he does not do something in this matter I will be very much disappointed. I am playing my last card now and if I lose the game it will be too bad. I will have to go home and tell the fishermen in my constituency that I have asked the Minister of Finance to put this right and that he has refused to do so. I trust that I will not have to do that.

I would suggest to the
minister that he might arrange the difficulty that my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has spoken of. Cordage and rope less than 1$ inches in diameter is now on the free list for use in the lobster fishery and if he will put manilla marlin for use in the lobstery fishery on the free list it will meet the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to the recital of his troubles by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. 'Sinclair) it puts me very much in mind of a line from Hamlet that I heard the other night:
One woe doth tread upon another's heels.
I have had due regard to what the hon. member for Guysborough draws to my attention and I have taken occasion to look into this matter of lobster twine recently. There is a statement which my hon. friend ha3 made which I think he will withdraw
when the facts which I have before me are brought to his attention. I have understood him to say that the present Government made a ruling which had not been adopted during the late Government's period of office in respect to the matter of this duty upon twine.
These are the facts. On the 18th of March, 1909, the collector of customs at Yarmouth advised the department that this twine was also used by furniture manufacturers and iron foundries in tying packages for shipments i and on the 26th of March, 1909, the collector was advised that such twine, although used for lobster traps, was not entitled to free entry. On the 14th of March, 1911, the collector of customs at Chatham forwarded a letter to the Department of Customs, inquiring as to the tariff classification of this twine when used for lobster traps. He was advised on the 18th of March, 1911, that it was dutiable. The ruling made in December, 1911, was in accordance with decisions previously given. I have made some inquiries and have been informed, although I do not pretend to have exhausted my inquiries in the matter, that it is almost impossible to place this twine upon the free list with the limitation that it is to be free when used for the fishing business, because once it has found its way into the hands of the retail dealers, it is quite impossible to follow it, so that it would really be making it free for all purposes.
We have the same provision in connection with ropes for lobster fishing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised by the customs officers that, in their opinion, it would be impossible to follow the twine in question. The effect of placing it upon the free list for the purpose that my hon. friend has in mind would be that it would be practically free for all purposes. I intend to pursue my inquiries further, and I will give the matter careful consideration before the final revision of the tariff takes place. At the present time I am unable to accede to the request of my hon. friend and place this twine on the free list for the reasons that I have given.

I am obliged to the minister for his explanation. I did not intend to mislead the committee about the facts. I did not have the information that prior to 1911 any inquiry had been made about the matter; but I was aware that a circular, which got into the press and was sent to all
I suppose the greatest difficulty will be that the country merchants who put the price down on the basis of its being imported and the buyer, as a rule, are under no special obligation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
546. Jute cloth or jute canvas, uncoloured, not further finished than cropped, bleached, mangled, or calendered-British preferential, 7J per cent; intermediate, 10 per cent; general, 10 per cent.
Will the minister please explain whether there is an increase in the duty upon these articles; and if so, the reason offered for the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This matter is a little difficult to explain. Will my hon. friend look at tariff item 545, which reads:
Jute and jute butts, jute cloth as taken from the loom, not coloured, cropped, mangled, pressed, calendered, not finished in any way; and jute canvas, free.
The change made is due partly to the fact that it is required for administrative purposes, because it is difficult to distinguish jute canvas from jute cloth. This item 545 formerly included jute canvas, uncoloured, without any limitation. As jute canvas is jute cloth, the Department of Customs in January, 1912, ruled that jute canvas, uncoloured, not further finished than cropped, bleached, mangled or calendered, was free. The ruling practically cancelled item 546. The change now made removes any doubt as to the intention of Parliament. In item 546 of the tariff resolutions, the words ' on jute canvas ' have been added after the words ' jute cloth1 and jute canvas uncoloured, not

further finished than cropped, bleached, mangled or calendered, become subject to a general tariff of ten per cent.
And for the last year you have not been collecting that duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, and jute canvas is
now dutiable whereas before it was not.

Is there any reason for that?
Mr.WHITE: No, except that it cannot he distinguished from jute cloth and there is the same reason for a duty on jute canvas as there is for a duty on jute cloth. I suppose the ordinary principle of reasonable protection would apply.
Has this anything to do with the manufacture of bags?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think so, but, frankly, I do not know a great deal about jute canvas and jute cloth. The change is made as much for administrative purposes as any other.

This matter was drawn to my attention through a gentleman, who said that he rather expected it would be dealt with in committee by the minister himself. He informs me that it will affect bag manfacturing, and so will affect the users of bags. The principal point to which he drew attention was in connection with the shipment of grain from the West. If grain is shipped westward for transit by the Panama canal, I think it is admitted that it will have to be bagged. Therefore a duty on this raw material for bags may form quite an item as against not only the bag manufacturers but the grain producers as well. As a matter of fact, it was the hon. member for Huntington (Mr. Robb) who brought me the information, and he being a leading miller is quite an authority. The party who brought it to his attention said he had made representations to the minister, who, he expected, would deal with it in committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No objection has been raised to this change on behalf of any hag manufacturer. Under item 252 of the tariff bags or sacks of hemp, linen or jute are dutiable at 20 per cent. I am not increasing that duty. I imagine there is no danger of an increase in the price of bags, because those manufacturers like others will be charging such prices as they are able to obtain for their product. I can-

not conceive that the imposition of a small duty on jute or canvas will have an appreciable effect upon the price of bags.

Do not the bagmakers
use jute imported free under item 545?

That is the intention. I brought this matter up the other night, and it was explained that the reason why there were these two items instead of the one item in the existing tariff, was that some manufacturers were bringing in jute canvas further manufactured than is allowed under section 545 because the custom houses were construing the clause improperly in some places.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: This is to make it plain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And I will draw attention to the fact-I believe it to be 11 p.m. a fact, though I am not positive-that in the case of such exports of grain as the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) speaks of, a drawback is granted.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
548. Twine or yarn of paper when imported by manufacturers of furniture for use only in their own factories in the manufacture of furniture-British preferential, free; intermediate, free; general, free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The purpose of this change is to bring about uniformity with item 724 of the present tariff which provides that this article is to be admitted free when imported to be ' woven into fabrics' in Canadian factories. I am advised that it was intended that this should cover the case of manufacturers of furniture, but the words ' woven into fabrics ' are not applicable to the processes in which the furniture manufacturer uses this twine. The change is designed to include manufacturers of furniture, widening the item to that extent.	.
It would be on all fours with the case I was putting to the minister in regard to fishing twine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But this could be much more readily checked up, the hon. gentleman will admit.
Perhaps so.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
575. Embroideries, n.o.p., lace, n.o.p., braids, n.o.p., tapes of cotton or linen not over one and one-quarter inches in width, not including measuring tape lines, fringes, n.o.p., cords, elastic, round or flat, garter elastic, tassels, handkerchiefs of all kinds, lace collars and all manufactures of lace, nets and nettings of cotton, linen, silk or other material, n.o.p., shams and curtains, when made up, trimmed or untrimmed, corsets of all kinds, linen or cotton clothing, n.o.p.-British preferential, 25 per cent; intermediate, 32^ per cent; general, 35 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have included here
all braids, n. o. p., and tapes of cotton or linen. This change is made partially for administrative purposes; the increase in revenue will not be considerable. These tapes are made by the Belding Paul Corti-celli Company and other manufacturers in Canada, and it is almost impossible, I am told, to distinguish between the tapes and the braids. So we have placed tapes in the item.
Mr. .BOIVIN:	I see the word 'garter
elastic.' But I understand there is another item in the tariff which covers elastic over one inch width on which the duty is 20 per cent. Can the minister tell me the reason for this difference of duty between 35 per cent on narrow elastic and 20 per cent on elastic slightly wider?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a matter my hon. friend drew to my attention in connection with webbing used for the manufacture of suspenders. Is that what he has in mind?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Respecting the request for additional duty on webbing used in the manufacture of suspenders and other articles, the manufacturers of suspenders contend that, owing to the large variety of designs or patterns of webbings required in their industry, it would not warrant the establishment of a factory in Canada to manufacture said webbings. The webbings form the component material of chief value in the manufacture of suspenders. It was, therefore, considered advisable to leave this matter over for attention when general revision of the tariff takes place. There was another matter to which my hon. friend drew attention.

The other matter was
giving relief to the manufacturer of this elastic either by giving him a drawback or allowing him a free entry for cotton yarns used in the manufacture of elastic. I see that under this tariff jute yarn, hemp yarn, linen yarn and woollen yarn are admitted free when used by Canadian manufacturers for the production of different articles.
Application has been made to the depart-

ment-it has undoubtedly been considered, although no change has been made in the tariS-for the placing of cotton, yam on the free list in order that it may be used in the manufacture of elastic fabric. It is admitted by the cotton manufacturers that what they call] combed yam and mercerized yarn is not manufactured in Canada and cannot be obtained in this country. Coarse cotton yarn, is produced in small quantities in only one factory in Canada, that of the Dominion Textile Company, I think. I understand that the minister hag in his department a letter from that firm saying that they have used their entire output and have none for sale1. There is in my constituency a factory engaged in the manufacture of elastic webbing. Four years ago elastic webbing was not manufactured in Canada; at the present time there i3 a factory at Granby-the Granby Elastic Webbing Company-and, I understand, one at Hamilton; these are the only two in Canada. The reason given by the hon. minister a moment ago for not increasing the duty on the wider fabric is a very good one, because that would increase the price to the suspender manufacturer and he in turn would be obliged to increase the price to the public. Of course, as the minister has said, it is only when the Budget is brought down that we are supposed to get from him information concerning the different changes in the tariff, but I would pcint out that this application has been before the department for almost two years; that two Budgets have been brought down and that we have never received ajjy information. I would ask the minister if he could not give this matter his consideration with a view to seeing whether these cotton yarns could not be1 placed upon the free list. If he. cannot, he should tell the committee now, in order that I may be in a position to transfer the information to the stockholders of this company, why this yam is not to be placed upon the free list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am obliged to my hon. friend for the information which he has given me. He is, no doubt, aware that no tariff changes are announced Or no information given with respect to the modification of tariff rates except in the Budget speech. Facts are brought to the attention of the Minister from time to time and requests are made for tariff action. I frequently receive letters from

parties-and their names are legion-asking me what I propose to do with regard to their requests, and my answer, couched always in very courteous terms, is that they will have to wait until tariff announcements are made in the Budget. The matter to which my hon. friend draws my attention might, I think, be dealt with in two ways. It might be dealt with in the Budget or it might be dealt with by Order in Council, because the Governor in Council, has the power, under existing legislation, to reduce or to remove the duties upon articles which enter into the manufacture of Canadian products. All that I can say to my hon. friend at the present moment-and I am sure that he will acquit me of any discourtesy-is that I shall be glad to give the matter careful consideration with a view to seeing whether or not anything can be done in the premises.

I quite understand that the hon. minister cannot make any announcement of tariff policy to-night or at any other time, except in the Budget speech, but I thought in view of the fact that the request had been refused, that the reason for that refusal might be given. That would not be a tariff announcement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a matter as complicated as the tariff, it is not feasible to give reasons for a refusal, because such diametrically opposite views exist with respect to tariff changes that on that ground alone it is not well that such reasons should be reduced to writing. My hon. friend will have to rest content with the answer which I give to all other parties making requests with regard to tariff matters: That if the Government has any announcement to make it will be either in the Budget or by action of the Order in Council. That is all that any Minister of Finance is able to say with respect to inquiries regarding tariff matters.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Did I understand the hon. member for Shefford to say that the people manufacturing this material could not get combed yarn in Canada?
Mr. BO'IVIN: I am not a member of the company, nor have I any direct interest in the undertaking, but I have been informed by the manager of the concern that it is impossible to get in Canada combed yarn for the manufacture of elastic webbing.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may be interested to learn that it may be

obtained in large quantities from the Dominion Cotton Company.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
577. Silk in the gum or spun silk, when imported by manufacturers of silk thread, silk underwear or of woven labels, for use exclusively in the manufacture of such articles in their own factories-British preferential, free; intermediate, free; general, free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I desire to change the
wording of this item so that it will read as follows:
Silk in the gum or spun silk when imported by manufacturers of silk underwear or of woven labels and spun silk, when imported by manufacturers of silk thread, when used exclusively for the manufacture of such artcles in their own factories, free.
Item as amended agreed to.
575. Embroidery, n.o.p., lace, n.o.p., braids, n.o.p.. etc.-British preferential, 25 per cent; intermediate, 32J per cent; general, 35 per cent.
Will that interfere with the cost of raw materials to the manufacturers of suspenders in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not. We are simply inserting tapes because they cannot be distinguished for administration purposes from braids. I do not think it is an important item. No objection has been raised as far as I know to its inclusion in this item.
I had an inquiry from a manufacturer in my own town asking about it and I was not prepared to say what the effect would be.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
651a. Buttons of vegetable ivory, per gross- British preferential, 5 cents and 20 per cent; intermediate, 5 cents and 30 per cent; general, 5 cents and 30 per cent.
Why is it necessary to add this high specific duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is due to the fact that manufacturers of buttons from vegetable ivory in Canada are subject to keen competition from Austria and Germany, the product of Austria being entitled to entry under the intermediate tariff. We have increased the rates on these buttons of vegetable ivory with a view of making conditions less trying to the Canadian manufacturer. I think it is a necessary change.
It seems to me that the specific duty added to the thirty per cent ad valorem makes a very high rate.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
On resolution No. 5-prohibited goods:

The Customs Department ought to be careful that the officers know an aigrette when they see it. I was on a train and the customs officer was inclined to take a cheap plume from a lady, thinking, from the minister's speech, that it was one of the articles prohibited.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In item 1023 I want to omit after the word ' bars ' the words ' or turned and polished shafting so that the item will read:
Rolled hexagon iron or steel bars when used in the manufacture of cold drawn or cold rolled iron or steel bars.
Why are those words being left out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me I will give that information to-morrow. It is so technical that I shall have to consult the experts. There are two resolutions, Nos. 29 and 31, of Government orders that relate to the tariff. I am advised that they may be taken up by the Committee of Ways and Means. I would ask if you, Mr. Chairman, or Mr. Speaker, see any objection to this course. They relate to the drawback provision in respect to duties paid on pig-iron imported into Canada and entering into the production of articles exported by Canadian manufacturers and into the manufacture of mowers, reapers and binders. It is my intention, because I think it inadvisable to have two tariff Bills in one session, that No. 31 should be included in this resolution so that all may be embodied in one Bill. No. 29 is a separate matter and will be covered by a separate Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be prepared to give information on resolutions 29 and 31 if the House desires it.
Is not the explanation practically what we have been discussing to-night; it synchronizes with what we have been debating. You have to have those resolutions in order to carry out your tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. 31 is a resolution relating to the Customs tariff, and I am advised that I can move it now. My hon. friends opposite, I think, understand my object in making this change, which is for the purpose of benefiting the steel industry. Manufacturers of goods for export into which pig-iron enters as a basic mate-

rial, and manufacturers of the articles mentioned in this resolution 31 on the Order Paper, who are entitled to a drawback in respect of their manufactures of mowing machines, reapers, harvesters, binders and attachments for binders, find it to their advantage to buy all their pig-iron from abroad rather than in Canada. It is at their request and after they have directed the attention of the Government to this matter on more than one occasion that we have decided to bring down this legislation. I explained it rather fully on the occasion of the Budget, and I do not think it is necessary to go into it now. The only question now is a matter of procedure. I would ask that Order No. 29 be not included in these resolutions, as it is an amendment to the Customs Act. No. 31 is an amendment to the Customs tariff, and it is the latter that I am anxious to have covered by the Bill which I shall introduce in respect to these resolutions, so that it will suffice, Mr. Chairman, if you include in the resolutions Order No. 31 on the Order Paper.

I did not catch the effect of the minister's amendment to item 1023, where he struck out the words ' or turned and polished shafting.' Does that mean that the manufacturers of shafting shall not get a drawback?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The information I have is that rolled hexagon iron or steel bars are not used for shafting.
Resolutions reported, read the first and the second time and concurred in.
On motion of Mr. White, the House adjourned at 11.33 p.m.
Friday, May 1, 1914.
